title: Teaching Bioinformatics in Low-resource Settings
text:
Overview
Teaching Bioinformatics in Low-resource Settings is an intensive train-the-trainer programme tailored for educators, researchers, clinicians, and core facility managers in resource-constrained environments—including Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs). While traditional bioinformatics pedagogy presumes high-speed, unmetered internet, institutional High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters, and uniform, modern student hardware, trainers in low-resource environments must navigate severe bandwidth limitations, frequent power interruptions, outdated and heterogeneous laptops, and adult learners facing acute terminal anxiety.
This course bridges the pedagogical and operational divide by integrating evidence-based adult learning theory with practical computational design. Participants learn how to construct offline-resilient, containerised curricula using micro-datasets, implement active learning strategies (such as participatory live coding and driver-navigator pairing), design authentic assessments, author publication-grade open courseware with Quarto, guide learners on the responsible use of generative AI, and nurture sustainable local communities of practice.






TipLearning Objectives



After completing this course, participants will be able to:

Apply Adult Learning Principles: Contrast andragogical principles with pedagogical assumptions, identify cognitive load thresholds, and mitigate terminal anxiety in adult wet-lab learners.
Implement Active Teaching Strategies: Facilitate participatory live coding with deliberate mistake handling, faded examples, and driver-navigator pair programming to maximise learner retention.
Engineer Defensive Computing Environments: Architect robust training setups resilient to power outages and internet dropouts using micro-datasets, static binaries, pre-cached container images (Apptainer/Docker), and offline conda-pack archives.
Design Cohesive Curricula: Formulate backward-designed instructional units using observable Bloom’s taxonomy action verbs, diagnostic multiple-choice questions with targeted distractors, and authentic capstone assessments.
Author and Publish Open Courseware: Create modular, version-controlled, and FAIR-compliant training materials using Quarto, Markdown callouts, GitHub Pages, and offline static site bundles.
Integrate Responsible AI: Guide students to critically leverage generative AI as a 24/7 virtual tutor while enforcing verification protocols against hallucinations, deprecated syntax, and genomic privacy violations.
Establish Communities of Practice: Overcome post-workshop regression and the “lone bioinformatician syndrome” by launching local peer-learning cohorts, hacky hours, and institutional study groups.
Deliver a Training Blueprint: Pitch a complete, peer-reviewed, and context-adapted bioinformatics training proposal equipped with contingency matrices and delivery logistics.




Target Audience
This course is engineered for:

Current and Aspiring Bioinformatics Educators: University lecturers, research software engineers, and teaching assistants preparing to deliver computational genomics or data analysis courses in low-resource or LMIC institutions.
Wet-Lab Scientists and Clinicians: Molecular biologists, clinical microbiologists, and laboratory heads transitioning into data analysis who wish to mentor colleagues and trainees.
Core Facility and Institutional Leads: Facility directors, systems administrators, and capacity-building coordinators tasked with rolling out scalable, sustainable bioinformatics training in regional research institutes.



Prerequisites
To gain the most from this train-the-trainer curriculum, participants should have:

Foundational Knowledge: Basic familiarity with molecular biology concepts (DNA, RNA, proteins, sequencing workflows) and standard bioinformatic data formats (e.g. FASTA, FASTQ, SAM/BAM, VCF).
Basic Command-Line Exposure: Familiarity with navigating directories (cd, ls, pwd) and viewing text files in a Unix-like shell is advantageous, though no advanced shell scripting or programming experience is required.
Educational Motivation: An active commitment to teaching, institutional capacity development, and open-source scientific knowledge dissemination.

title: 1  Course Introduction
text:
1.1 Welcome to Teaching Bioinformatics in Low-resource Settings
Welcome to Teaching Bioinformatics in Low-resource Settings. This course is not a standard bioinformatics workshop where you learn how to assemble a genome or call variants. Instead, it is an intensive train-the-trainer programme designed to transform subject-matter specialists (researchers, core facility analysts, clinicians, and university lecturers) into resilient, empathetic, and effective bioinformatics educators.
Worldwide, bioinformatics has transitioned from a niche academic sub-discipline into the backbone of modern life sciences, clinical diagnostics, and public health surveillance. However, the vast majority of bioinformatics educational resources and training methodologies originate in high-income research hubs. These curricula routinely take foundational infrastructure for granted:
When trainers attempt to transplant these high-resource curricula directly into low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) or under-resourced regional institutions, the training frequently breaks down. Instructors encounter unexpected infrastructure challenges: download commands fail halfway through due to insufficient bandwidth, outdated student laptops run out of RAM and power cuts terminate running pipelines.
This course aims to demonstrate that world-class bioinformatics training does not require advanced infrastructure. By combining modern, evidence-based learning theory with well thought out computational design, you will learn how to build training programmes that are pedagogically empowering, technically robust, and fully sustainable in any setting.

title: 1  Course Introduction
section: 1.2 The Double Hurdle of Low-Resource Instruction
text:
1.2 The Double Hurdle of Low-Resource Instruction
Educators in resource-constrained environments confront a unique dynamic. In a standard classroom, learners face only one primary challenge: mastering the academic curriculum. In low-resource settings, both instructors and students must clear two distinct hurdles simultaneously:

Table 1: Additional challenges faced in low-resource settings






1. Pedagogical & cognitive
2. Infrastructural & material




• Abstract command-line syntax
• Rolling blackouts & power cuts


• Going from an expert to a novice
• Severe bandwidth & download caps


• Acute terminal anxiety
• Heterogeneous, low-specification laptops


• Cognitive load overload
• Windows CRLF / permission bugs


• Heavy clinical/wet-lab burdens
• Absence of institutional HPC/IT



1. The Pedagogical and Cognitive Hurdle
Learners in your training may be professionals: senior microbiologists, physicians, parasitologists, or postgraduates. In their laboratories or clinics, they command respect. When seated in front of a Unix terminal, a single confusing error message (command not found, permission denied, or SyntaxError) can induce terminal anxiety leading to imposter syndrome. If instructors rush through commands or take over keyboards, learners may disengage and conclude that bioinformatics is a discipline reserved for computer scientists.
2. The Infrastructural and Material Hurdle
Simultaneously, the technical foundation beneath the classroom can be shakey. Bandwidth is rarely sufficient for 25 simultaneous conda install or apt-get downloads. Electricity may cut out without warning. Student laptops vary from decade-old dual-core Windows machines with 4 GB of RAM to locked institutional laptops that prohibit software installation.
As an educator in these settings, your job is not merely to transmit technical knowledge; every lesson you deliver must be engineered to anticipate failure and potentially succeed entirely offline.

1.3.1 Part 1: Principles of Bioinformatics Training Design (Chapters 2–9)
We begin with the theoretical side of teaching (pedagogy) and material development:

Learning Theories: Understanding Knowles’ principles, managing cognitive load, and dismantling the “Expert-Novice Paradox”.
Active Teaching Methodologies: Mastering participatory live coding, faded examples, and driver-navigator pair programming.
Classroom Orchestration: Cultivating psychological safety, managing helpers with the “hands-off-keyboard” rule, and timing with the Rule of Thirds.
Curriculum Architecture: Applying Wiggins & McTighe’s Backward Design framework with observable Bloom’s taxonomy action verbs.
Lesson Planning & Delivery Logistics: Structuring lesson arcs, applying the double-time rule, and building contingency matrices.
Diagnostic Assessments: Creating multiple-choice questions with diagnostic distractors.
Responsible Use of AI: Guiding learners to treat Large Language Models as 24/7 virtual tutors while rigorously guarding against hallucinations, deprecated syntax, and data leakage.



1.3.2 Part 2: Building Practical and Scaleable Bioinformatics Training (Chapters 10–17)
Next, we explore how to adapt computational bioinformatics content for resource-constrained environments:

Open Educational Resources: Repurposing high-quality curricula from The Carpentries, Galaxy Training Network (GTN) and H3ABioNet.
Containerisation: Utilizing Docker and rootless Apptainer/Singularity (.sif) to package dependencies for offline USB distribution.
Software Installation: Avoiding Conda dependency solve lockouts using Micromamba and portable conda-pack offline bundles.
Cloud & HPC Economics: Navigating the “Data Locality Rule”, preventing cloud bill shock, and teaching HPC cluster etiquette through SLURM queue mechanics.
Micro-datasets: Downsampling gigabyte-scale sequencing libraries into 2-megabyte classroom datasets that run in under 60 seconds on modest laptops.
Authoring Open Courseware: Packaging FAIR-compliant, portable learning materials with Quarto, Markdown callouts, and offline static site bundles.
Case Studies: Discussing how to adapt existing training materials to your context.



1.3.3 Part 3: Design your Training (Chapters 18–19)
Finally, you will synthesize everything you have learned into building a plan for delivering training in your institution:

The Training Design Sprint: You will design a complete, customized bioinformatics training plan for your home institution and pitch it to your peers and instructors for feedback.
Communities of Practice: Strategies to overcome post-workshop attrition, dismantle the “lone bioinformatician syndrome”, and launch sustainable local study groups and Hacky Hours.

1.4 Interactive Exercise: Assessing Your Teaching Ecosystem






ExerciseExercise 1 - Establishing Your Baseline Teaching Profile






Before diving into pedagogical theory, let us map the real-world conditions under which you currently teach or plan to teach. Take 10 minutes to answer the following four questions:

Target Cohort: Who are your future learners (e.g. wet-lab MSc students, clinicians, university faculty)? What is their computational starting baseline?
Hardware Reality: What devices will your learners bring (personal Windows laptops, shared desktop computer labs, institutional MacBooks)? Do they possess local administrative rights (sudo/admin)?
Connectivity & Power: How reliable is the internet bandwidth and electrical grid at your target training venue? Can your course be run entirely offline?
Primary Pedagogical Obstacle: What is the single biggest bottleneck you have observed in bioinformatics training at your home institution (e.g. software installation collapse, cognitive overload, post-workshop abandonment)?







AnswerAnswer






Your Baseline Teaching Profile
Notice that almost every trainer in low-resource settings identifies similar bottlenecks:

Hardware Heterogeneity: Most students arrive with Windows machines carrying different antivirus software and minimal RAM, making unstandardised installations painful.
Administrative Lockouts: Trainees using hospital or institutional laptops often cannot install Docker or Miniconda without institutional IT intervention.
Losing Time to Installation”: In many traditional workshops, the entire first day is lost to troubleshooting package dependencies, leaving students exhausted before any biological concepts are introduced.
Post-Workshop Isolation: Students leave inspired, but within two weeks hit an unexplained error on their own data and give up because they lack local peer support.

Keep your answers close at hand. Throughout this course, you will refine these notes into your master training plan in Chapter 18.

title: 2  What is Bioinformatics?
text:
2.1 Introduction: Defining Bioinformatics
At its core, bioinformatics is an interdisciplinary field that develops and applies computational, mathematical, and statistical methods to store, manage, analyse, and interpret biological data.
The term was coined in 1970 by Paulien Hogeweg and Ben Hesper to define “the study of informatic processes in biotic systems”. Today, bioinformatics has evolved into an indispensable component of the biological sciences. It transforms vast amounts of raw data, such as nucleotide sequences, protein structures, and mass spectra, into actionable biological knowledge.
Bioinformatics is often confused with related terms. As a trainer, helping your learners distinguish between these terms builds clarity and sets realistic expectations:
In practice, these disciplines overlap heavily. A working bioinformatician frequently switches between the roles of software user, pipeline engineer, data analyst, and biological interpreter.

title: 2  What is Bioinformatics?
text:
What is bioinformatics?









NoteDisentangling Related Terminology




Bioinformatics: The development and application of computational tools, databases, and pipelines to manage and analyse large biological datasets (e.g. sequence alignment, variant calling, RNA-seq quantification).
Computational Biology: The development and application of data-analytical and theoretical methods, mathematical modelling, and computational simulation techniques to study biological systems (often more theory- and model-driven).
Biostatistics: The application of statistical methods to biological and medical experiment design, data collection, and inference (focussing heavily on hypothesis testing, confounding factors, and clinical trials).
Data Science: An umbrella term encompassing statistics, data engineering, machine learning, and domain-specific knowledge to extract patterns from structured and unstructured data.

title: 2  What is Bioinformatics?
text:
2.2 The Foundational Pillars of Bioinformatics
To be an effective practitioner, and an effective trainer, you must recognise that bioinformatics is supported by three distinct pillars. An imbalance among these three pillars is one of the most common causes of difficulty for learners:

Biological Domain Knowledge: Bioinformatics is driven by biological questions. Without an understanding of molecular biology, experimental design, and the limitations of laboratory assays (e.g. library preparation biases, PCR duplicates, sequencing platform error profiles), computational analysis becomes an exercise in blindly running commands. As trainers, we must align computational steps back to the biological question: Why are we trimming reads? What does an alignment score signify biologically?
Computational and Software Skills: Biological data files are typically too large to open in spreadsheet applications like Microsoft Excel. Bioinformaticians rely on the Unix/Linux command-line environment, scripting languages (Python and R), file format standards (FASTQ, FASTA, SAM/BAM, VCF, GFF/GTF), version control (Git), and containerisation (Docker, Singularity/Apptainer). Mastery of these tools allows researchers to handle data systematically, automate multi-step analyses, and ensure reproducibility.
Statistical and Quantitative Rigour: Modern ’omics technologies generate high-dimensional data where the number of measured features (e.g. 20,000 genes) far exceeds the number of biological replicates. Understanding concepts such as multiple testing correction (e.g. False Discovery Rate), normalisation strategies, batch effects, and statistical power is critical to prevent spurious discoveries.

section: 2.3 Why Bioinformatics Matters in Low-Resource Settings
text:
2.3 Why Bioinformatics Matters in Low-Resource Settings
Bioinformatics offers us the opportunity to democratise scientific discovery and public health surveillance, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs):
1. Tackling Local Health and Agricultural Priorities
Low-resource regions often bear the heaviest burdens of endemic infectious diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, cholera, HIV, and neglected tropical diseases, emerging epidemic outbreaks, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and climate-induced food insecurity.
Locally driven bioinformatics empowers researchers and public health agencies to:

Track transmission routes and outbreaks in real time using pathogen genomics.
Identify novel mutations linked to drug resistance or vaccine escape.
Characterise local crop and livestock varieties to breed climate-resilient strains.
Catalogue and preserve regional biodiversity.

2. Dismantling “Helicopter/Parachute Science”
Historically, many research initiatives in LMICs followed an extractive model: samples were collected locally, exported to institutions in high-income countries for sequencing and analysis, and published with minimal or purely nominal local participation.
Building local bioinformatics capacity flips this power dynamic. When local scientists possess the expertise to analyse and interpret their own data, they retain ownership of biological resources, drive the research agenda based on national priorities, and translate findings directly to local healthcare and agricultural policies.
3. High Scientific Impact with Modest Capital Investment
Building and maintaining wet laboratories requires continuous investments: specialized reagents, expensive consumables, reliable cold-chain storage, and costly equipment service contracts.
In contrast, bioinformatics leverages computational power, open-source software, and globally shared public repositories (e.g. NCBI, EBI, GISAID). A single computer with skilled analytical talent can conduct world-class discovery science, re-analyse published datasets, and generate publishable insights without requiring millions of dollars in laboratory infrastructure.

section: 2.4 Realities and Constraints in Low-Resource Environments
text:
2.4 Realities and Constraints in Low-Resource Environments
While the promise of bioinformatics is vast, performing and teaching bioinformatics in resource-constrained environments presents unique practical hurdles. As an educator, your training design must directly account for these real-world constraints rather than ignoring them.
1. Technical and Infrastructural Barriers

Unreliable or high-Cost Internet Bandwidth: Live downloads of large reference genomes or raw sequence data (FASTQ files) often fail, choke institutional connections, or incur high cellular data costs.
Unreliable power supply: Unscheduled power outages can terminate ongoing pipeline runs and disrupt classroom sessions unless uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) or cloud-hosted sessions are used.
Hardware Limitations: Learners frequently bring personal laptops with modest specifications (e.g. 4–8 GB RAM, dual-core processors, limited disk space, 32-bit or older Windows systems) which cannot execute memory-heavy tools like standard genome aligners or de novo assemblers.
Absence of Local HPC Facilities: Many universities and institutes lack dedicated High-Performance Computing clusters, system administrators, or stable server environments.

2. Educational & Human Capital Barriers

Unbalanced Curricular: Biological science curricula in many institutions rarely include foundational computer science, Linux command line, or programming. Trainees are often exposed to computation for the first time during postgraduate studies.
The “Lone Bioinformatician”: Many trainees return from workshops to departments where they are the sole individual with computational skills, lacking local peer support, code review, or experienced mentorship.
High Attrition: Skilled computational personnel are frequently recruited away by international organisations or private industry, leaving local institutions in a cycle of constant capacity rebuilding.







ImportantBioinformatics training for wet lab and clinical scientists



Learners from wet-lab or clinical backgrounds face two challenges to their learning simultaneously:

Conceptual Complexity: Learning abstract biological and statistical algorithms (e.g. de Bruijn graphs, hidden Markov models, Bayesian phylogenetics).
Technical Challenges: Interacting with a computer via a text-only terminal, understanding absolute vs. relative file paths, handling syntax errors, and managing command flags.

If both challenges are presented at once with complex, large files, mental overload occurs quickly. Effective training separates these challenges and builds competence incrementally.

title: 2  What is Bioinformatics?
text:
2.5 Rethinking Training for Low-Resource Settings
Standard bioinformatics training materials created in well-resourced institutions often make implicit assumptions: gigabit internet, institutional Linux clusters, powerful Mac/Linux laptops, and uninterrupted power. When delivered unchanged in resource-limited settings, these courses frequently stumble.
As trainers, we must adopt resource-aware pedagogy:







Conventional Training Assumption
Resource-Aware Pedagogical Strategy




“Download this 1 GB FASTQ file”
Use micro-datasets (downsampled to a few thousand reads) that execute in seconds on a basic laptop.


“Run this tool on our local HPC cluster”
Teach using lightweight environments: local containers, lightweight virtual machines, or portable web-based interfaces.


“Install software via complex compilation”
Pre-configure environments (Conda/Mamba, Docker/Singularity) or provide self-contained sandboxes.


“Follow this 50-step copy-paste script”
Focus on conceptual understanding: input files, understanding parameters, output interpretation and troubleshooting.


“Look up documentation online”
Provide offline-accessible documentation, cheatsheets, and pre-cached local resources.

text:
2.6 Interactive Reflection & Discussion
To design effective training, you must first understand the reality of your learners’ environment and identify potential stumbling blocks.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Assessing Trainee Realities and Context






Think about the specific group of learners you plan to train in your institution or region.

Hardware & OS: What operating systems and hardware configurations do your learners typically possess?
Connectivity: How reliable is the internet connection in your training venue? Can you rely on live internet downloads during class?
Prior Experience: Have your participants ever used a command-line interface (CLI) or terminal before?
Actionable Adaptation: Identify one potential point of failure during a live hands-on workshop and describe how you would design an offline fallback.







HintHint






Consider common issues such as 30 students trying to download a 200 MB reference genome at the same time, or Windows laptops lacking a native Unix environment.










AnswerAnswer







Hardware & OS: In many LMIC settings, over 80% of learners use Windows laptops with 4–8 GB RAM. Recommended strategies include using WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux), web-based platforms, or lightweight Linux live USBs.
Connectivity: Never rely on live downloads during a workshop. Trainers should pre-load all datasets, software packages (or container images), and documentation onto shared USB thumb drives or a local classroom server (e.g. Raspberry Pi or local Wi-Fi router).
Prior Experience: Most life-science learners have never used the terminal. Dedicate time to core navigation (cd, ls, pwd) and models of the filesystem before introducing bioinformatics tools.
Offline Fallback: Always maintain pre-computed intermediate and final output files. If an assembly or alignment tool fails or runs too slowly on a participant’s laptop, they can immediately load the pre-computed output and continue with downstream interpretation without falling behind.















ExerciseExercise 2 - Deconstructing a Command: The Learner’s Perspective






Consider a standard bioinformatics command introduced in an introductory genomics tutorial:
fastp -i sample1_R1.fastq.gz -I sample1_R2.fastq.gz \
      -o trimmed_R1.fastq.gz -O trimmed_R2.fastq.gz \
      --detect_adapter_for_pe --html sample1_fastp.html -w 4
List at least four distinct computational concepts or hidden assumptions that a wet-lab biologist must understand in order to run and modify this command successfully.






AnswerAnswer







Working Directory & File Paths: The learner must understand that sample1_R1.fastq.gz must exist in the current directory, or else provide relative/absolute paths.
Command Syntax & Flags: The learner must recognise that -i, -I, -o, -O, and -w are flags (arguments) modifying how fastp operates, and that case sensitivity matters (-i vs -I).
Line Continuations (\): The backslash is a shell continuation character. Typing a space after the backslash causes syntax errors that confuse novices.
Hardware Resources (-w 4): The -w 4 flag requests 4 worker threads. On a dual-core laptop, this can cause sluggishness or confusion about what “threads” mean.
Output Redirection & Formats: The command produces both compressed sequence files (.fastq.gz) and an HTML report (.html), requiring an understanding of how to view each file type.

Lesson for Trainers: Deconstruct commands step-by-step and explain the syntax anatomy before asking students to modify them.

Bioinformatics is a multidisciplinary science combining biological knowledge, computational skills, and statistical rigour to turn biological data into meaningful insights.
In low-resource settings, bioinformatics is a powerful equalizer, allowing impactful research, disease surveillance, and scientific independence with minimal wet-lab capital expenditure.

title: 3  Learning Principles
text:
3.1 Pedagogy versus Andragogy
When designing training for researchers, university lecturers, laboratory technicians, or clinicians, instructors often fall back on the teaching models they experienced during primary or secondary school: an authoritative instructor delivering a lecture from the front of the room, followed by standardized tests.
In professional training, this traditional teacher-centred approach frequently leads to disengagement, frustration, and poor retention.
Even though the term “pedagogy” is colloquially used in academic discourse as a general synonym for teaching, this course strictly adopts an andragogical framework.

title: 3  Learning Principles
text:
NoteDefining the Terms




Pedagogy: Literally “to lead the child” (from the Greek paid, child, and agogos, leading). It describes the art, theory, and methods of teaching children, where the instructor assumes full responsibility for determining what will be learned, how it will be learned, when it will be learned, and if it has been learned.
Andragogy: Literally “to lead the adult” (from the Greek aner, adult). Popularized by Malcolm Knowles in 1968, andragogy refers to the art and science of helping adults learn. It recognizes that adults learn through fundamentally different psychological motivations, experiences, and cognitive frameworks than children.





Pedagogy vs Andragogy in bioinformatics






Pedagogy (Child / Traditional)
Andragogy (Adult Learning)




Learner is dependent on teacher
Learner is self-directed


Teacher controls content & pace
Learner shares control & goals


Learner brings little experience
Rich reservoir of domain experience


Subject-centred (curriculum)
Problem-centred (real research)


External motivation (grades)
Internal motivation (career/publications)


Passive content absorption
Active, experiential facilitation

title: 3  Learning Principles
text:
3.2 Knowles’ Core Assumptions of Andragogy
Malcolm Knowles and colleagues (2015) identified core assumptions that distinguish adult learners. Understanding these assumptions allows bioinformatics instructors to design empathetic, highly effective training programs:
1. The Need to Know
Adults need to know why they need to learn something before undertaking to learn it. They resist learning things simply because an instructor says “it’s on the syllabus.”

In Bioinformatics: Never introduce a tool (e.g. fastp or samtools) with raw syntax alone. First demonstrate the problem: “Here is an unaligned read file with adapter contamination. If we don’t trim these sequences, 15% of our reads will fail to map to the reference genome, wasting your sequencing budget.”

2. The Learner’s Self-Concept
Adults need to be perceived as self-directed, autonomous individuals. When placed in situations where they are treated like passive schoolchildren or talked down to, they may experience cognitive friction and resentment.

In Bioinformatics: Avoid rigid, lockstep dictation. Give learners autonomy over project choices, choice of example datasets, and space for exploratory debugging.

3. The Role of Learner Experience
Adults enter the classroom with a vast reservoir of prior professional and personal experience. This experience is a rich resource for learning, but it also carries entrenched mental models and cognitive biases.

In Bioinformatics: Tap into their wet-lab knowledge. An experienced molecular biologist already understands PCR amplification, primer design, and DNA denaturation. Connect computational steps directly to the physical benchwork they already master:

Quality scores \(\rightarrow\) Gel electrophoresis band clarity.
Read alignment \(\rightarrow\) Hybridization of primers.
PCR duplicates \(\rightarrow\) Over-amplification on the thermal cycler.


4. Readiness to Learn
Adults become ready to learn things when they experience a need to know them in order to cope with real-life situations, career requirements, or research challenges.

In Bioinformatics: Trainees rarely attend workshops for abstract curiosity; they attend because they have sequencing data sitting on a hard drive that they cannot analyze, or a grant review demanding computational validation. Align workshop exercises with their immediate professional needs.

5. Orientation to Learning
Children are subject-centred (e.g. “We are studying History or Mathematics today”). Adults are problem-centred or task-centred.

In Bioinformatics: Structure lessons around authentic scientific questions: “Can we identify the transmission cluster in this hospital outbreak?” rather than “Chapter 3: The Syntax of BCFtools.”

6. Motivation
While adults respond to external motivators (e.g. promotion, certificates, higher salary), the most potent motivators are internal: job satisfaction, self-esteem, curiosity, and the desire to overcome a research barrier.

3.3 Shifting Roles: From Teacher to Facilitator
Applying andragogy requires redefining the instructor’s professional identity:

Table 1: Teacher versus facilitator






The Traditional Teacher
The Learning Facilitator




“I hold the knowledge”
“We co-construct knowledge”


Transmits fixed syllabus
Manages the learning process


Controls timing and content
Responds to learner needs


Evaluates and grades students
Promotes self-evaluation


Focuses on presentation skills
Focuses on relational & process design skills



Following Knowles et al. (2015), the facilitator prepares in advance an operational structure involving:

Preparing the learner: Setting clear, realistic expectations and demystifying prerequisites before Day 1.
Establishing an empathetic climate: Creating an environment where questions are welcomed and errors are celebrated as learning moments.
Mutual planning: Diagnosing learner needs and negotiating priorities.
Designing authentic learning experiences: Using participatory live coding, micro-datasets, and localized biological problems.
Evaluating and improving: Gathering continuous formative feedback (e.g. sticky notes, minute papers) to adapt the course dynamically.

title: 3  Learning Principles
text:
3.4 Andragogy in Low-Resource Environments
In low-resource settings, the principles of adult learning intersect with systemic socio-economic and institutional realities:

High Opportunity Cost: Adult professionals taking 3–5 days away from clinical wards, wet laboratories, or heavy teaching loads need to know their investment of time will immediately translate into tangible productivity. If a course wastes two days on failed installations, learners will disengage.
The “Lone Bioinformatician” Reality: Many adult trainees are the sole individual from their institution attending the course. They carry the immense burden of needing to return home and become the computational expert, mentor, and pipeline developer for their entire department.
Empowerment Through Local Relevance: Adult learners in LMICs are intensely motivated by solving regional health and agricultural problems (e.g. local AMR surveillance, malaria eradication, climate-resilient crop breeding). When instructors replace abstract examples with datasets reflecting their local reality, learning ceases to be an academic exercise—it becomes an act of scientific self-determination.

title: 3  Learning Principles
text:
3.5 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will challenge you to identify andragogical principles in action and transform traditional teacher-centred lessons into engaging, facilitator-led workshops.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Transforming a Teacher-Centred Lecture






You are reviewing an introductory lesson plan designed by a colleague for a two day variant-calling workshop for hospital microbiologists.
The current lesson plan reads:

“09:00 - 10:30: Slide presentation (60 slides) explaining the history of sequencing technologies, Sanger chemistry, Illumina sequencing-by-synthesis, and quality score logarithmic mathematical formulas. Trainer will lecture from the front; students listen quietly.”


Identify three specific ways this lesson plan violates Knowles’ assumptions of andragogy.
What emotional or cognitive state will this design trigger in adult clinical microbiologists?
Redesign this 90-minute block into an andragogically sound, facilitator-led learning experience.







HintHint






Consider the “Need to Know”, “Problem-Centred Orientation”, and the value of active, hands-on participation.










AnswerAnswer






3.5.1 Andragogical Redesign

Violations of Andragogy:

Passive Transmission (Pedagogical): Treats learners as empty vessels to be filled with historical theory rather than self-directed practitioners.
Lack of “Need to Know”: Memorizing Phred logarithmic math formulas (\(P = 10^{-Q/10}\)) in the abstract has zero immediate relevance to clinical practice.
Subject-Centred, Not Problem-Centred: Focuses on the history of sequencing instead of the clinical challenge the microbiologists care about.

Likely Learner Reaction: Boredom, fatigue, cognitive overload, and anxiety: “Why am I sitting through 60 slides of history when I have patient samples to analyze? Is bioinformatics just endless theory?”
Facilitator-Led Redesign:

09:00 - 09:15 (The Clinical Hook): Start with an authentic patient case study: “A patient in our ICU has a hospital-acquired infection resistant to carbapenems. We sequenced the isolate. How do we know if our sequencing data is reliable enough to make a clinical decision?”
09:15 - 09:40 (Interactive Exploration): Open a real FastQC report on screen. Have trainees explore the report in pairs. Ask them: “Where does the quality drop? What does this red warning mean?”
09:40 - 10:10 (Targeted Explanation): Briefly explain Phred quality scores and Illumina error profiles in response to what they just observed on their screens.
10:10 - 10:30 (Hands-on Action): Trainees run a read-trimming command on a micro-dataset and compare the “before” and “after” quality reports with their partner.
















ExerciseExercise 2 - Navigating the Expert-Novice Paradox in Live Classrooms






During the afternoon practical, Professor K., a distinguished 55-year-old professor of virology, is attempting to change directories in the terminal. They type cd data and receive bash: cd: data: No such file or directory.
Professor K. visibly stiffens, crosses their arms, pushes their laptop away, and stops participating. When a roving helper approaches, Professor K. mutters: “This computer interface is useless nonsense. In our wet lab, we generate real data; this is just academic games.”

What psychological dynamic is Professor K. experiencing?
Why is defensive frustration a common coping mechanism for senior adult experts learning computation?
How should the instructor/helper respond to de-escalate the tension, restore psychological safety, and re-engage Professor K.?







AnswerAnswer






3.5.2 Facilitator Intervention

Psychological Dynamic: Professor K. is experiencing acute cognitive vulnerability and loss of self-concept. As a senior, highly respected virologist, having a computer tell them they made a mistake (“No such file or directory”) threatens their professional identity and sense of competence.
Why Defensive Frustration Occurs: When adult experts feel deskilled, dismissing the subject (“useless nonsense”, “academic games”) is a natural psychological defense mechanism to protect self-esteem and deflect perceived inadequacy.
Facilitator Response:

Validate Domain Expertise First: Empathize and reaffirm their high status: “Professor K., you are completely right that wet-lab data generation is the foundation of all biology. Without your viral culture work, bioinformatics has nothing to compute.”
De-escalate the Error: Demystify the error as a mechanical miscommunication, not an intellectual failure: “The terminal is completely literal and a bit stubborn. It only says ‘No such file’ because our current working directory is one level above where the folder sits. It’s like dialing a phone number missing one area code.”
Guide, Don’t Take Over: Never grab their keyboard! Guide them verbally: “Let’s type pwd together to see where we are… Perfect. Now type ls to see what is in this room… Ah, look, the folder is called raw_data. If we type cd raw_data, it will jump right in.”
Affirm Success: When it succeeds: “Excellent! Now your sequencing reads are right in front of you.”

TipKey Points




Andragogy Governs Adult Learning: Adult learners are self-directed, bring vast reservoirs of domain experience, and learn best when knowledge is problem-centred, immediately applicable, and internally motivated.
Connect Computational Syntax to Wet-Lab Concepts: Ground abstract command-line concepts in the physical biology they already understand (e.g. connecting quality scores to gel electrophoresis or PCR duplicates to over-cycling).

title: 4  Strategies for Training
text:
4.1 Introduction: Moving Beyond Passive Instruction
Traditional academic instruction relies heavily on lectures: an instructor displays static presentation slides while students passively take notes. In computational biology, this approach consistently produces poor learning outcomes.
A student can watch 50 slides explaining read alignment or Python syntax, yet find themselves completely paralyzed the moment they face a blank terminal window.
Teaching bioinformatics effectively, especially to life scientists in low-resource settings, requires active pedagogical strategies where learners construct mental models through immediate physical practice, real-time feedback, and structured collaboration.

title: 4  Strategies for Training
text:
4.2 Participatory Live Coding
Participatory live coding, pioneered by The Carpentries, is the gold standard instructional technique for teaching programming and the command line.
Instead of displaying code on slides, the instructor shares their terminal or code editor on the big screen and types every command live in real time while students type along simultaneously on their own machines.

Table 2: Principles of Participatory Live Coding


Instructor Screen
Learner Screen




1. Explain the biological goal
Understand context


2. Type command deliberately
Type along simultaneously


3. Press Enter & examine output
Observe matching output


4. Intentional typo / bug!
Diagnose error together




4.2.1 Rules of Effective Live Coding

Enlarge Your Screen Font: Set your terminal or editor font size to at least 18pt–24pt. Ensure dark text on a light background or high-contrast themes so learners in the back of the room can read every character.
Never Type in Silence: Narrate everything you do before and while typing. Say: “I am going to type fastp, followed by a space, then -i for input file…”
Pace Yourself Deliberately: Remember that novice learners must split their attention between looking at your screen, looking at their own screen, and typing on their keyboard. Slow down your natural typing speed by at least 50%.
Use Tab-Completion Visually: Announce every time you press Tab to auto-complete a file path. This reinforces essential habits and prevents typing errors.
Celebrate and Diagnose Typos: When you make an accidental typo (or make a deliberate one), do not quickly erase it in shame. Use it as a teaching moment: read the error message aloud with the room and walk through the diagnostic steps.

title: 4  Strategies for Training
text:
4.3 Paired Programming: The Driver-Navigator Model
In many low-resource workshops, class sizes are large (25–40 students) while teaching assistants or helpers are scarce (often just the instructor and one assistant).
Paired programming is a collaborative learning technique adapted from software engineering that dramatically improves learning retention and reduces the burden on instructors.



The Driver-Navigator model



4.3.1 Why Pair Programming Excels in Resource-Constrained Classrooms

Solves Hardware Shortages: If an institutional computer lab has only 12 functional computers for 24 students, paired programming turns a deficit into a learning advantage.
Reduces Reliance on Helpers: Pairs catch 80% of syntax errors (missing spaces, typos, wrong slashes) between themselves before raising their hands, freeing helpers to focus on deeper conceptual misunderstandings.
Peer Tutoring and Social Learning: Pairing a slightly more experienced student with a complete novice builds confidence in both: the novice receives immediate, non-judgmental guidance, while the experienced student solidifies their knowledge by explaining it.

text:
4.4 Scaffolded Learning: Using Faded Examples
When introducing a new computational pattern (such as writing a for loop or parsing a VCF file), novices may experience cognitive overload if asked to write code completely from scratch on a blank screen.
Cognitive psychology research shows that faded examples provide the most effective scaffolding for technical learning:



Using Faded Examples


By gradually fading the scaffolding, learners build confidence and autonomy instead of nervously staring at a blank screen.

A central team of expert instructors broadcasts lectures and live demonstrations via low-bandwidth video conferencing.
Each participating institution hosts an in-person physical classroom staffed by local facilitators.
Exercises are performed on standardized local virtual machines or container environments.

title: 4  Strategies for Training
text:
4.6 Cognitive Load Management: The 15-Minute Rule
The human working memory has severe capacity limits, holding only four to seven novel chunks of information at once. In a technical workshop, cognitive overload sets in quickly if an instructor lectures continuously.






ImportantThe 15 Minute Instructional Rule



Never lecture or live-code for more than 15 consecutive minutes without a pause, active learner action, or formative check. Break every 90-minute workshop session into short, interactive cycles:

7–10 mins: Live coding / conceptual framing.
3–5 mins: Micro-exercise / prediction challenge (“What will happen if I run this?”).
2 mins: Debrief and sticky-note check.

text:
4.7 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will help you practice designing active learning interventions and managing live coding sessions.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Designing a Faded Example Sequence






You are teaching a group of wet-lab microbiologists how to use grep to extract specific genes from a GFF3 annotation file.
Create a three step faded example sequence that takes learners from a fully worked demonstration to an independent task:

Provide the fully worked initial example.
Create a partially faded example with clear blanks and instructions.
Formulate an independent challenge task.







HintHint






Ensure the progression tests the same conceptual pattern (searching by feature type or attribute) while gradually removing syntax hints.










AnswerAnswer






4.7.1 Three Step Faded Example

Step 1: Fully Worked Example (Instructor demonstrates live):
# Find all ribosomal RNA (rRNA) features in the annotation file
grep "rRNA" annotations.gff > results/rRNA_features.gff
Step 2: Partially Faded Example (Learners complete):
# Find all transfer RNA (tRNA) features and save to results/tRNA_features.gff
grep "________" annotations.gff > results/________.gff
Step 3: Independent Challenge: “Now, write a single command from scratch that searches annotations.gff for all CDS (coding sequence) features, counts how many there are, and prints only the count to the terminal screen.” (Solution: grep -c "CDS" annotations.gff or grep "CDS" annotations.gff | wc -l)















ExerciseExercise 2 - Managing Differences in Student Pacing During Live Coding






During a live-coding session on Bash navigation, you observe that three learners with prior computer science exposure are typing ahead, finishing tasks in 30 seconds, and looking bored. Meanwhile, five clinical researchers who have never used a terminal are struggling with file paths and falling 10 minutes behind.

Why is continuing at the pace of the fast learners a mistake?
What concrete pedagogical strategies can you use to keep advanced learners engaged without abandoning novice learners?
How can pair programming resolve this specific classroom tension?







AnswerAnswer






4.7.2 Facilitator Intervention

Don’t Follow Fast Learners: Advanced learners naturally speak up, type quickly, and nod when asked “Is everyone ready?”. If the instructor paces the class to these few vocal students, the remaining 80% of the room becomes lost, gives up, and mentally checks out.
Strategies for Fast Learners:

Provide “Bonus Challenges” / Stretch Goals: Add an optional extension question at the bottom of every exercise: “Finished early? Try modifying your command to sort the results alphabetically by gene name.”
Use Them as Peer Helpers: Ask advanced students to assist their immediate table neighbors: “If you have a green sticky note up, look to your left and right and help your neighbor debug their path.”

Pair Programming Solution: Pair the advanced learner (as Navigator) with the novice learner (as Driver). The advanced student cannot touch the keys; they must verbally explain the computational logic, deepening their own understanding, while the novice gains hands-on muscle memory and personalized support.

title: 5  Elements of Effective Training
text:
5.2 Human Support: Helpers/Facilitators
The most significant predictor of a smooth computational workshop is not how well the instructor delivers the materials, but the presence of roving helpers (facilitators).



Classroom Support Topology



5.2.1 One Helper per 6–8 Learners
In a room of 25 participants, having a single instructor trying to teach while running around the room fixing individual syntax errors brings the entire workshop to a stop.

Maintain a ratio of one helper for every 6 to 8 students.
Helpers can be postgraduate students, local bioinformaticians, or alumni of previous workshops.







ImportantThe Hands-Off-the-Keyboard Rule



The single most important rule for workshop helpers: when helping a struggling student, NEVER take their keyboard or mouse away from them.

If you grab their keyboard and type the fix in 5 seconds, you demonstrate your competence, not theirs. The student learns nothing and feels disempowered.
Instead, place your hands behind your back. Guide the student verbally: “Look at line 3. Do you see a missing space after the comma? What happens if you add a space and run it again?”
Let the student’s own fingers type the correction and experience the triumph of solving the problem.

5.3 Physical & Technical Logistics in Low-Resource Venues
In low-resource venues, environmental and logistical failures can derail training faster than software bugs. An effective trainer audits the venue before learners arrive:

Low-resource venue audit checklist






Category
Practical Verification Step




1. Electrical Power
• Count physical wall outlets vs. students• Bring 4–6 heavy-duty multi-plug extension cords• Verify venue generator / UPS backup status


2. Display & Screen
• Test projector resolution and brightness• Adjust blinds/curtains to prevent sun glare• Enlarge terminal font to 18pt–24pt


3. Connectivity
• Bring dedicated mobile 4G/5G Wi-Fi hotspot reserved exclusively for the instructor• Pre-load all data & tools onto USB drives


4. Comfort & Audio
• Check room acoustics; use a microphone if room exceeds 25 participants• Ensure adequate ventilation and drinking water









WarningThe Laptop Battery Crisis



Bioinformatics pipelines (e.g. alignment, assembly, trimming) run CPU cores at 100% capacity. An ordinary consumer laptop that lasts 5 hours during web browsing will drain its battery in 45–60 minutes during a practical! If learners cannot plug in their chargers, the afternoon session will collapse as laptops shut down.

text:
5.4 Pacing and Time Management: The Rule of Thirds
The most common mistake made by new trainers is curriculum bloat, cramming five days’ worth of content into a two day schedule. Rushing through slides to “finish the training” produces cognitive overload and reduces learner retention.

5.4.1 The Rule of Thirds
Structure your workshop schedule around three balanced allocations:



The Rule of Thirds


Always plan to deliver 20% less content than you think you have time for. Mastering foundational navigation, file manipulation, and quality control thoroughly is far more valuable to a beginner than skimming superficially through advanced variant calling pipelines.

title: 5  Elements of Effective Training
text:
5.5 Continuous Formative Feedback
How do you know if the room is following your instruction or completely lost? Never ask: “Does everyone understand?” (Shy learners will not speak up, and confident learners will nod).
Deploy two proven formative feedback mechanisms:
1. Two-Color Sticky Notes (Real-Time Telemetry) Give every learner two sticky notes (Green and Red):

Green on laptop lid: “I have completed the task and my code worked.”
Red on laptop lid: “I am stuck or encountered an error; I need a helper.”

This allows the instructor to scan the room in one second: if 70% of the room has red stickies up, the instructor knows to pause immediately and address a universal issue on the main screen.
2. The Daily Synthesis At the end of each day (or before the lunch break), give learners three minutes to answer two anonymous questions on a sticky note or online form:

What was the most important concept or skill you learned today?
What is still confusing or causing you anxiety?

Read these responses in the evening. At the start of the next morning, spend the first 15 minutes directly addressing the most confusing points. This builds trust and ensures misconceptions are corrected before new content is introduced.

title: 5  Elements of Effective Training
text:
5.6 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will test your ability to manage classroom dynamics and utilize formative feedback to adjust your teaching.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Training Your Workshop Helpers






You are recruiting two postgraduate students from your university to serve as helpers for an upcoming three day introductory genomics workshop. Neither has ever served as a facilitator before.

Write a four bullet-point briefing guide detailing how helpers should interact with struggling learners during hands-on practicals.
What specific instruction will you give regarding the “Hands-off-the-keyboard” rule?
How should helpers communicate with the main instructor during class if they notice a widespread systemic problem (e.g. everyone’s Wi-Fi failing or a corrupted download)?







HintHint






Focus on learner empowerment, body language, and non-disruptive classroom signaling.










AnswerAnswer






5.6.1 Helper Briefing Guide

Core Helper Guidelines:

Move around the room: Walk slowly through the aisles and scan for red sticky notes or distressed body language (frowning, crossed arms). Do not sit at the back checking your phone.
Adopt approachable posture: Kneel down or pull up a chair next to the student so your eyes are at their level. Standing over someone while they struggle can feel intimidating.
Guide verbally, never take keys: Explain what is wrong and guide their fingers to type the solution. Never touch their mouse or keyboard.
Keep explanations concise: Solve the immediate blockage and encourage the student to continue. Do not launch into a 15-minute theoretical digression.

Hands-Off-the-Keyboard Instruction: “If you touch a student’s keyboard, you rob them of the ‘Aha!’ moment of fixing their own code. Keep your hands behind your back or hold a notepad. Tell them what to look for, ask questions, and let them type the solution themselves.”
Communicating Systemic Problems: Helpers should not shout across the room or wait until the end of the day. If two consecutive students encounter the exact same error (e.g. a missing reference file or broken link), the helper should walk up to the instructor’s podium and whisper: “Pause for a second - everyone in Row 2 is getting a permissions error on sample1.fq.”















ExerciseExercise 2 - Analyzing Daily Feedback






At the end of Day 1 of your Linux and sequencing QC course, you collect feedback on sticky notes from 20 participants.
When reviewing the responses, you notice:

12 students wrote: “I loved FastQC, but I still do not understand what absolute and relative paths mean, and cd .. is making me confused.”
5 students wrote: “The pace in the afternoon was too fast; I couldn’t keep up with typing.”


How should you adjust your lesson plan for the start of Day 2 based on this feedback?
How should you address this feedback transparently with the class the next morning?
Outline a 10-minute classroom activity for the opening of Day 2 to clear up the “muddiest point” (paths and cd ..).







AnswerAnswer






5.6.2 Responsive Action Plan

Schedule adjustment:

Cut or compress the least critical afternoon topic planned for Day 2 to create a 30-minute buffer.
Slow down live-coding typing pace by 30% and institute mandatory sticky note checks after every three commands.

Transparent morning address: “Good morning everyone! Thank you for your feedback yesterday. Over half of you mentioned that relative paths and cd .. are still confusing you, and that our typing pace was too quick in the afternoon. Thank you for telling me! Today, we are slowing down, and we are going to spend our first 15 minutes mastering paths physically on the whiteboard until everyone feels 100% confident.”
10 Minute Physical Activity (Spatial Mental Model):

Draw a large directory tree on the physical whiteboard (/ root, home/, user/, projects/, data/).
Give a student an eraser or magnetic marker representing the terminal cursor (pwd).
Have the room call out: “Where does the cursor land if we type cd data? What happens if we type cd ..?”
Let students physically move the marker up and down the tree on the board until the spatial concept clicks before opening laptops.

title: 6  Designing Training
text:
6.1 Introduction: The Classic “Forward Design” Approach
When asked to design a new bioinformatics workshop, instructors often begin by listing software tools:
This approach, known as Forward Design, is driven by content rather than learning. The instructor decides what tools they want to demonstrate, and creates lectures around tool syntax. The issue with this is that at the end of the course, the students may be unable to analyze their own research data independently.
Backward Design (Wiggins & McTighe, 2005) reverses this process. By starting with the final intended competencies and working backward, instructors create tightly integrated, purposeful training programs where every lecture, exercise, and dataset directly serves a measurable objective.

title: 6  Designing Training
section: 6.2 Stage 1: Learner Personas — Knowing Your Audience
text:
6.2 Stage 1: Learner Personas — Knowing Your Audience
You cannot design an effective curriculum for “anyone interested in bioinformatics.” A 50 year-old hospital pathologist has fundamentally different technical baselines, career incentives, and hardware constraints than a 22 year-old master’s student in computer science.
A Learner Persona is a short, fictional archetype (profile) that embodies the characteristics, prior knowledge, motivations, and potential difficulties of your target audience.



Anatomy of a Learner Persona



6.2.1 Why Personas Drive Critical Design Decisions
When planning your curriculum, consult your persona to resolve pedagogical debates:

“Should we teach how to compile BCFtools from C source code?” \(\rightarrow\) Look at Dr. Amina: No! She lacks root permissions and needs to solve a clinical problem, not learn software engineering. Provide a pre-built static binary or container.
“Should we use a 15 GB human exome dataset?” \(\rightarrow\) Look at Dr. Amina: No! Her laptop has 8 GB RAM and her focus is bacterial AMR. Use a 2 MB locus-targeted bacterial micro-dataset.

text:
6.3 Stage 2: Formulating Measurable Learning Outcomes
Once you know your audience, define what they should be able to achieve. Use Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy to align your learning objectives with the appropriate cognitive level:

Table 2: Bloom’s taxonomy for bioinformatics







Level
Description
Action Verbs to Use




6. Create
Design new workflows, pipelines or automated solutions
Construct, assemble, automate, formulate


5. Evaluate
Judge data quality or justify analytical choices
Assess, appraise, validate, critique


4. Analyze
Differentiate true signal from technical artifacts; filter data
Distinguish, diagnose, troubleshoot, filter


3. Apply
Execute commands and pipelines on novel datasets
Run, execute, modify, calculate, implement


2. Understand

Differentiate, outline, summarize, predict


1. Remember
Recall syntax, flag meanings, and directory structures
Identify, list, recall, name, state









WarningAvoid “Zombie Verbs”



Never write learning objectives with vague, unmeasurable verbs:

❌ “Learners will understand Linux.” (How do you measure “understand”?)
❌ “Learners will be exposed to variant calling.” (Exposure does not mean competence).
❌ “Learners will appreciate high-throughput sequencing.”

Use Observable Action Verbs:

✅ “Learners will execute read trimming using fastp and critique post-filtering quality metrics.”
✅ “Learners will diagnose Out-Of-Memory errors in SPAdes and adjust thread and memory parameters accordingly.”

title: 6  Designing Training
text:
6.4 Stage 3: Determining Acceptable Evidence (Assessment First)
In Backward Design, before you write a single slide or choose a tutorial, ask yourself: “How will the learners and I know that they have achieved the learning outcome?”
Design your summative challenge or end-of-module practical first:

Desired Outcome: “Learners will be able to identify antimicrobial resistance mutations in a bacterial isolate.”
Acceptable Evidence (Assessment): Provide learners with a raw paired-end micro-dataset of an uncharacterized Klebsiella isolate. Give them 45 minutes to run QC, map reads to a reference contig, call variants, and report which antibiotic the strain is resistant to.
Instructional Plan: Now design the specific live coding sessions, faded examples, and command deconstructions needed to equip them for that challenge!

text:
6.5 Concept Mapping: Mapping Dependencies
Bioinformatics learning is strictly hierarchical. You cannot teach read mapping before learners understand file paths; you cannot teach variant filtering before they understand VCF columns.
A Concept Map is a visual diagram connecting concepts with labeled relationship arrows. Building a concept map reveals hidden dependencies:



Example concept map


If an instructor tries to teach quality trimming without verifying that students understand relative paths, the lesson will collapse into the troubleshooting of No such file or directory errors.

6.6 Designing with Low-Resource Constraints as First Principles
In low-resource environments, constraints are not bugs; they are fundamental design parameters:

Constraint-first curriculum design






Constraint
Design Rule




1. Zero Internet Guarantee
Curriculum must execute 100% offline from local USB drives or pre-loaded classroom mirrors.


2. 4 GB RAM Ceiling
No tool or dataset may require > 2 GB RAM (reserving 2 GB for the operating system).


3. Non-Root Lab Permissions
Tools must run in user space (static binaries, Micromamba environments, or Apptainer).


4. Modular Schedule
Break curriculum into self-contained 2-hour modules that can survive sudden power outages.

title: 6  Designing Training
text:
6.7 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will guide you through building a learner persona and mapping a backward-designed module.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Creating a Contextualized Learner Persona






You are tasked with designing a three day workshop titled “Practical Pathogen Genomics for Outbreak Surveillance” to be held at a public research institute in West Africa.
Develop a complete Learner Persona for this course by specifying:

Name, Age, and Professional Role.
Biological Domain Expertise vs. Computational Baseline.
Primary Motivation (Why are they taking time away from work to attend?).
Three Specific Technical / Infrastructural Constraints they will bring to the classroom.







HintHint






Make the persona realistic and multidimensional. Include hardware, network, and institutional restrictions.










AnswerAnswer






6.7.1 Model Learner Persona

Identity:

Name: Dr. Jean-Paul (Age: 34).
Role: Medical Epidemiologist at the National Public Health Laboratory.

Expertise & Baseline:

Domain: Expert in infectious disease surveillance, diagnostic RT-PCR, and clinical epidemiology during cholera and viral hemorrhagic fever outbreaks.
Computational: Uses Windows 11 daily for Excel and Epi Info; has never opened a terminal, written a script, or run a Linux command.

Motivation:

His laboratory recently acquired an Oxford Nanopore MinION to sequence cholera and mpox isolates locally. Currently, raw sequencing files are sent abroad for analysis, delaying outbreak response by weeks. He needs to run local QC, assembly, and lineage assignment within 24 hours of sequencing.

Constraints:

Hardware: Uses an older institutional Windows laptop with 6 GB RAM and only 25 GB of free hard drive space.
Permissions: Does not have administrator/root access to install software on his work laptop.
Connectivity: Works in an office with frequent 2-to-3-hour power cuts and relies on an intermittent cellular hotspot with expensive data limits.
















ExerciseExercise 2 - Applying Backward Design to a Variant-Calling Module






A training team submits a draft module titled “Introduction to Variant Calling”. The current plan starts with a 45-minute lecture on the math of Bayesian variant probability, followed by running a 10-line GATK Bash script.
Apply the three stages of Backward Design to restructure this module:

Stage 1 (Desired Results): Formulate two Bloom-aligned, measurable learning outcomes.
Stage 2 (Acceptable Evidence): Design a hands-on assessment task that proves learners achieved those outcomes.
Stage 3 (Learning Plan): Outline the learning activities and micro-datasets required to prepare them for that assessment.







AnswerAnswer






6.7.2 Backward Design Blueprint

Stage 1: Desired Learning Outcomes:

“Learners will execute variant calling on a bacterial micro-dataset using bcftools.” (Bloom: Apply)
“Learners will filter raw variant calls to eliminate low-depth and strand-biased artifacts, validating candidate drug-resistance SNPs in IGV.” (Bloom: Evaluate)

Stage 2: Acceptable Evidence (Assessment Task):

Provide trainees with an alignment BAM file of a candidate resistant M. tuberculosis isolate.
Task: Generate a filtered VCF file containing only variants with \(\text{QUAL} \ge 30\) and \(\text{DP} \ge 15\), open the candidate mutation in IGV, and submit a 2-sentence clinical diagnosis stating whether the isolate carries the Rifampicin resistance mutation.

Stage 3: Learning Plan & Scaffolding:

Activity 1: 15-minute live coding deconstructing VCF columns (CHROM, POS, REF, ALT, QUAL, INFO).
Activity 2: Faded example exercise constructing a bcftools filter command.
Activity 3: Visual demonstration in IGV comparing an authentic mutation against a sequencing error.
Dataset: 1.5 MB locus-targeted BAM file of the rpoB gene cassette that executes in 10 seconds.

text:
6.8 Summary






TipKey Points




Begin with the End in Mind: Backward Design guarantees that every lecture, tool, and practical directly serves measurable student competencies rather than lists of commonly used software.
Anchor Design in Real Personas: Create learner personas that reflect real-world technical baselines, professional incentives, and institutional hardware constraints.
Use Measurable Action Verbs: Eliminate vague “zombie verbs” (understand, appreciate); use Bloom’s Taxonomy verbs (execute, diagnose, differentiate, validate) to define observable outcomes.
Assess Before You Teach: Design the summative challenge and evidence of competence before drafting presentation slides.
Map Dependencies Explicitly: Use concept maps to diagnose prerequisite bottlenecks and prevent cognitive leaps in the classroom.
Design for Constraints: Treat limited bandwidth, low RAM, and lack of root permissions as primary architectural design parameters from day one.

7.1 Introduction: The “Know-it-all” Instructor
Experienced bioinformaticians often believe that because they have run a pipeline hundreds of times in their research, they can walk into a classroom and teach it without a detailed plan.

title: 7  Lesson Planning
text:
7.2 Structuring Your Lessons
Every modular session of your training (typically 60 to 90 minutes) should follow a structured pedagogical progression:



Six stage lesson plan


Stage 1: The Motivation (5 Minutes)
Never start with syntax. Start with the biological or operational problem:

“Imagine you receive a call from the local hospital’s epidemiologist: three infants in the neonatal ward have contracted multidrug-resistant Serratia. We need to determine if they share an identical strain within the next two hours. How do we extract that answer from raw sequencing data?”

Stage 2: Objective & Mental Model Framing (5 Minutes)
Clearly state the single capability learners will gain. Draw a 3-box workflow on the whiteboard: \[\text{Raw FASTQ} \xrightarrow{\text{fastp (Trimming)}} \text{Clean FASTQ} \xrightarrow{\text{fastp.html (Report)}}\]
Stage 3: Participatory Demonstration (15–20 Minutes)
Live-code the foundational command deliberately. Deconstruct the flags, press Enter together, and inspect the resulting output files with ls -lh and head.
Stage 4: Formative Hands-on Challenge (20–25 Minutes)
Learners immediately put hands to keys in pairs. They modify parameters, run a second sample, or fill in a faded template while helpers move around the room.
Stage 5: Collective Debrief & Error Deconstruction (10 Minutes)
Bring the room back together. Ask a learner to share what their report showed. Highlight a common bug that multiple students encountered during the exercise and explain why it occurred.
Stage 6: Cognitive Closure (5 Minutes)
Summarize the core mental model and preview what comes next: “Now that our reads are clean, in the next session we will map them to our reference genome.”

title: 7  Lesson Planning
text:
7.3 Time Budgeting: The “Double-Time Rule”
The single greatest planning failure in computational training is underestimating how long novice learners take to complete an exercise:






ImportantThe Double-Time Rule



Any computational exercise that takes an experienced instructor 5 minutes to type and execute will take novice learners at least 15 to 20 minutes (3x to 4x longer).



7.3.1 Why Novices Require 3x More Time:

Locating Windows: Switching between the browser tutorial, the terminal window, and file directories takes novices multiple clicks and spatial orientation time.
Keyboard Friction: Novices hunt for special characters like ~ (tilde), | (pipe), \ (backslash), and _ (underscore), which reside in different keyboard locations across international laptop layouts.
Typing Speed & Syntax Errors: Beginners average 15–20 words per minute and make typos that require helper intervention.
Tool Execution Latency: On older consumer laptops with 4 GB RAM, a tool runs 2–3 times slower than on an instructor’s high-spec MacBook or Linux laptop.

title: 7  Lesson Planning
text:
7.6 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will test your ability to construct realistic lesson timelines and prepare for live classroom contingencies.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Drafting a Time-Budgeted Lesson Plan






You have been allocated a 75 minute morning session to teach “Inspecting Alignments with SAMtools” to 20 master’s students in agricultural genomics.
Draft a detailed lesson plan that applies the six stage lesson plan:

Allocate specific minute-by-minute timings for each of the six stages.
Formulate the opening Motivation.
Detail the specific hands-on task for the learners during the formative challenge stage.
Specify where you will incorporate a deliberate five minute buffer.







HintHint






Remember the Double-Time Rule: keep the hands-on challenge focused and achievable within 20 minutes.










AnswerAnswer






7.6.1 75 Minute Lesson Plan Blueprint

Timeline Breakdown:

00:00 - 00:05 (Stage 1: Motivation): Show an outbreak of cassava mosaic disease. Explain why knowing whether sequencing reads map uniquely across viral strains dictates disease control.
00:05 - 00:10 (Stage 2: Objectives): Define learning outcomes: convert SAM to sorted BAM, index the file, and calculate mapping depth.
00:10 - 00:25 (Stage 3: Demonstration): Participatory live coding of samtools view -bS and samtools sort. Enlarge font; narrate the -@ and -o flags.
00:25 - 00:45 (Stage 4: Formative Challenge): Paired hands-on exercise (see below).
00:45 - 00:55 (Buffer / Catch-Up): Built-in 10-minute buffer for helpers to assist struggling pairs and ensure every laptop finishes.
00:55 - 01:05 (Stage 5: Collective Debrief): Examine flagstat results on screen; discuss why 12% of reads were unmapped.
01:05 - 01:15 (Stage 6: Closure & Key Points): Review key points; green stickies check; break.

Formative Hands-on Challenge: “Working with your partner, run samtools flagstat on cassava_sample2_sorted.bam. Write down: (1) What percentage of reads mapped successfully? (2) How many reads mapped as proper pairs? Post a green sticky when both questions are answered.”















ExerciseExercise 2 - Resolving a Live Classroom Emergency






At 14:15 on Day 2 of your workshop, a thunderstorm knocks out the power grid at your training venue. The room goes dark, the ceiling projector turns off, and the venue Wi-Fi router dies immediately.
Learner laptops have approximately 45–60 minutes of battery life remaining. Your schedule calls for a 2 hour practical on de novo genome assembly using SPAdes.

Why would attempting to run the planned SPAdes assembly practical on laptop batteries be a bad idea?
Formulate an immediate 45 minute “Plan C” emergency activity that continues active learning using remaining battery life without internet or heavy CPU computation.
How will you adjust the schedule once power returns?







AnswerAnswer






7.6.2 Emergency Response Protocol

Why SPAdes on Battery Fails: SPAdes is a CPU-intensive multi-threaded de Bruijn graph assembler that runs all processor cores at 100%. Running SPAdes will exhaust laptop batteries in 20 minutes, causing machines to shut down mid-assembly and corrupting files. Furthermore, without the projector, learners cannot follow live coding.
45-Minute “Plan C” Activity (Low-Power Data Interpretation):

Action: Instruct learners to immediately dim laptop screen brightness to 30% to conserve battery.
Activity: Pivot to an offline data interpretation and quality critique practical: “Everyone, open the pre-computed QUAST assembly report (quast_report.html) and BUSCO summary table located in your offline course folder. In pairs, compare Assembly A (standard parameters) versus Assembly B (relaxed k-mer parameters). Answer three questions: Which assembly has a higher N50? Which assembly has fewer misassemblies? Which one captures more complete core genes?”
Advantage: Opening static HTML reports consumes almost zero CPU/battery, requires zero internet, and shifts focus to high-value biological critique.

Schedule Adjustment: When power returns, do not attempt to make up the lost live assembly time by rushing. Skip the live assembly execution entirely, briefly review the command syntax on the whiteboard for 10 minutes, and proceed directly to downstream annotation using pre-computed assembly outputs.

Structure Protects Learning: Adhere to the six stage lesson layout (Motivation, Objectives, Demonstration, Challenge, Debrief, Closure) to keep sessions purposeful and engaging.
Budget with the Double-Time Rule: Novices require 3x to 4x longer than experienced instructors to complete computational tasks. Budget time accordingly.

title: 8  Assessment Strategies
text:
8.1 Introduction: Why Assessment is Not About Grading
In formal university education, assessment is often equated with examinations, grades, and rankings. When teaching professionals, such as researchers, clinicians, and laboratory scientists, traditional testing is counterproductive. It induces anxiety, triggers imposter syndrome, and discourages exploratory experimentation.
In short-format bioinformatics training, assessment serves a fundamentally different purpose: it is a diagnostic tool.
Formative assessment tells both the instructor and the learner: Was that concept understood? Do we share the same mental model? Can we move forward, or do we need to pause and clarify?

title: 8  Assessment Strategies
text:
8.2 Diagnostic Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs)
A standard multiple-choice question often tests trivial recall of facts. A diagnostic MCQ, in contrast, is designed to reveal specific misconceptions or flawed mental models.

8.2.1 The Anatomy of a Diagnostic MCQ
An effective diagnostic MCQ consists of:

A Clear Stem: A focused question presenting a concrete problem or command.
One Correct Answer: Unambiguously accurate.
Plausible Distractors (Wrong Answers): Each incorrect option represents a known, specific conceptual error or common beginner trap.







ImportantSample diagnostic bioinformatics MCQ



Question: You want to count how many sequences are in a multi-FASTA
file called isolates.fasta. Which command should you run?

wc -l isolates.fasta

grep -c ">" isolates.fasta

grep -c "^>" isolates.fasta

head -n 4 isolates.fasta





8.2.2 What Each Choice Diagnoses:

If they pick A (wc -l): Confuses total lines in a file with total sequences (forgets that FASTA sequences wrap across multiple lines).
If they pick B (grep -c ">"): Understands the header marker (>), but forgets that description headers or quality lines may contain > mid-line; misses the line-start anchor (^).
If they pick C (grep -c "^>"): CORRECT. Accurately identifies the start of header lines.
If they pick D (head -n 4): Confuses FASTQ 4-line records with FASTA format.







NotePeer Instruction (The Mazur Technique)



When running an MCQ in class:

Have students vote individually in silence.
If 40–70% get it right, do not give the answer away!
Tell students: “Turn to your neighbor. Find someone who picked a different letter, and convince them why your answer is correct (2 minutes).”
Re-vote. The percentage of correct responses almost always jumps to 85–90% through peer explanation!

title: 8  Assessment Strategies
text:
8.3 Parson’s Problems: Jumbled Code
One of the greatest pedagogical inventions in computing education is the Parson’s Problem (Parsons & Haden, 2006).
Novice bioinformaticians frequently struggle with simultaneous cognitive loads: remembering high-level pipeline logic while hunting for missing quotes, misplaced spaces, or exact flag syntax.
A Parson’s Problem eliminates syntax frustration by providing learners with the exact lines of code scrambled in random order. The learner’s task is simply to arrange the lines into the correct execution sequence.






ImportantParson’s Problem: variant calling workflow



Task: Put the following steps in the correct order to identify high-quality genomic variants from raw sequencing reads:
[ ] samtools index aligned_sorted.bam
[ ] fastp -i raw_R1.fq.gz -I raw_R2.fq.gz -o clean_R1.fq.gz ...
[ ] bcftools call -mv -Oz -o raw_variants.vcf.gz
[ ] bwa mem reference.fasta clean_R1.fq.gz clean_R2.fq.gz | ...
[ ] bcftools filter -e 'QUAL < 30 || DP < 10' raw_variants.vcf.gz


Correct Order:

fastp (Quality trimming raw reads)
bwa mem (Aligning clean reads to reference)
samtools index (Indexing the sorted BAM file)
bcftools call (Calling raw variants)
bcftools filter (Filtering low-quality calls)

Parson’s problems test whether students understand the data flow and logical dependencies of a pipeline without letting syntax typos derail their progress.
