title: 8  Assessment Strategies
text:
8.4 Zero-Bandwidth Classroom Assessment Techniques
In low-resource venues, modern web polling applications (such as Mentimeter, Kahoot, or Slido) often fail because classroom Wi-Fi is too slow or students lack cellular data bundles.
Use these zero-bandwidth, low-tech alternatives:

Table 2: Zero-bandwidth formative tools






Technique
How It Works in Practice




1. Finger Voting
For MCQs (A, B, C, D): Students hold 1, 2, 3, or 4 fingers against their chest. On count of three, everyone displays their vote simultaneously.


2. Sticky Note Bar Chart
Post a line on the whiteboard: [Hard] ── [Easy]. Students stick their colored sticky notes along the spectrum during coffee breaks.


3. Mini-Whiteboards or Paper Slips
Learners write a one-word command or path on a sheet of paper and hold it up simultaneously.


4. Think-Pair-Share
Give a 60-second prompt; pairs discuss for 2 minutes; call on two random pairs to share.









TipThe “Chest Vote” Rule



When conducting finger voting, have students hold their hand flat against their chest before displaying their fingers. This prevents slower students from looking around the room and copying the vote of the most confident student.

8.5 Authentic Assessment in Bioinformatics
Learners are motivated by authentic tasks that mirror their professional responsibilities. Replace artificial quizzes with authentic computational deliverables:

Table 3: Traditional versus authentic assessment






Traditional quiz
Authentic task




• “What is the flag for output in fastp?”• “Define N50 in one sentence.”
• “Generate a MultiQC report for these 4 patient samples and identify which sample failed library prep.”


• Memorization-focused
• Interpretation-focused

• Directly mirrors lab reality




8.5.1 Examples of Authentic Tasks:

The Outbreak Report: Give learners a VCF file of a clinical isolate; ask them to fill out a three field hospital report: (1) Pathogen species, (2) Detected AMR mutations, (3) Recommended treatment exclusion.
The Quality Audit: Provide three MultiQC reports; ask pairs to act as a core facility manager and decide: “Which of these three sequencing batches should we accept, and which should we reject and send for re-sequencing?”

section: 8.6 Measuring Impact: Pre- and Post-Workshop Surveys
text:
8.6 Measuring Impact: Pre- and Post-Workshop Surveys
To evaluate training efficacy and report outcomes to institutional funders, administer a Pre-Workshop Survey and an immediate Post-Workshop Survey.

8.6.1 Measuring Self-Efficacy (Likert Scale)
Rather than testing trivia, measure changes in learner self-efficacy (confidence in their ability to perform tasks independently):

“On a scale of 1 (Not at all confident) to 5 (Extremely confident), rate your ability to:”



Navigate directories and inspect files using the Linux command line.
Execute an automated quality-control pipeline on paired-end reads.
Troubleshoot a syntax error in the terminal independently.
Identify and filter technical artifacts in a variant call set.




8.6.2 Long-Term Impact Evaluation (3–6 Months Post-Course)
Follow up with participants months later to measure real-world translation:

Have you applied the tools taught in the workshop to your research?
Have you analyzed new datasets that contributed to a thesis, paper, or clinical report?
Have you taught or shared these computational skills with colleagues at your home institution?

title: 8  Assessment Strategies
text:
8.7 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will test your ability to design diagnostic distractors and build authentic assessments.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Designing a Diagnostic MCQ with Misconception Distractors






You are teaching a lesson on file paths in Linux. You want to assess whether learners understand the difference between absolute paths, relative paths, and the parent directory (..).
Write a diagnostic MCQ: 1. Provide a clear question stem based on an explicit directory tree. 2. Provide the correct answer. 3. Write three plausible distractors, explicitly stating what mental model misconception each distractor diagnoses.






HintHint






Use a simple tree where the user’s current working directory (pwd) is a subfolder like /home/trainee/projects/.










AnswerAnswer






8.7.1 Diagnostic MCQ Blueprint
Stem: Given the following directory structure:
/home/trainee/
├── data/
│   └── raw.fq
└── projects/  <-- (Current Working Directory: pwd)
You are currently inside /home/trainee/projects/. Which command will successfully display the first 5 lines of raw.fq?

Option A: head -n 5 /data/raw.fq
Option B: head -n 5 data/raw.fq
Option C: head -n 5 ../data/raw.fq (CORRECT)
Option D: head -n 5 raw.fq

Diagnostic Analysis of Distractors:

Option A: Diagnoses the misconception that / (root) is the same as the user’s home directory (~). The learner thinks /data is inside home, when in fact it is at the root level of the system.
Option B: Diagnoses a failure of spatial orientation. The learner assumes data/ is a child folder inside their current directory (projects/), forgetting they must first step up into trainee/.
Option D: Diagnoses the misconception common among GUI users: assuming the computer knows where raw.fq is regardless of directory coordinates.















ExerciseExercise 2 - Constructing an Authentic Final Assessment






Design an Authentic Assessment Activity for the final afternoon of a three day bacterial genomics workshop in a low-resource setting.
Specify:

The Scenario / Biological Persona.
The Provided Materials / Micro-dataset (size and format).
The Student Deliverable.
How this task assesses learning without relying on traditional written exams.







AnswerAnswer






8.7.2 Authentic Final Assessment Blueprint

The Scenario: “You are the bioinformatics officer at the regional hospital. Two blood culture isolates of Salmonella enterica were obtained from patients in Ward 4. The hospital infection control committee wants to know: Are these two cases part of the same nosocomial transmission event, or independent community acquisitions?”
Provided Materials:

Two paired-end micro-datasets (patientA_R1/R2.fq.gz and patientB_R1/R2.fq.gz, each 15 MB).
Reference genome FASTA file of Salmonella enterica.
A pre-compiled USB bundle containing fastp, bwa, samtools, and bcftools.

Concrete Deliverable: Pairs submit a one page Outbreak Briefing containing:

Summary table of raw reads, post-trimming Q30 percentage, and mapping rate for both isolates.
Total number of high-quality Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) differentiating Patient A from Patient B.
An IGV screenshot showing at least one distinguishing variant.
Final Recommendation: Is this a hospital outbreak (typically \(\le 5\) SNPs difference) or independent infections (\(> 50\) SNPs)?

Pedagogical Rationale: This task evaluates read QC, alignment, indexing, variant calling, variant filtering, visual inspection, and clinical interpretation simultaneously. It mirrors actual professional practice, engages adult intrinsic motivation, and requires no traditional grading.

Assessment Drives Learning, Not Grading: Use formative assessment during class as a real-time diagnostic navigation tool, not a ranking system.

title: 9  Responsible Use of AI
text:
9.1 Introduction: The “Virtual Mentor” in Low-Resource Settings
In well-funded research hubs, novice bioinformaticians are surrounded by experienced colleagues: postdocs down the hall, institutional core facilities, and dedicated Slack channels where they can ask for debugging advice.
In many low-resource institutions, however, researchers work as “lone bioinformaticians”. They are often the only person in their department attempting to run high-throughput sequencing pipelines. When an analysis throws a cryptic stack trace or an environmental error, they have no local mentor to turn to.
Generative Artificial Intelligence (Large Language Models such as Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and local open-source models) can serve as a transformative equalizer. It acts as a tireless, personal tutor that can explain error messages, generate initial pipeline templates, and demystify Linux commands.
However, like any powerful laboratory instrument, AI can produce catastrophic results if used without rigorous calibration, verification, and ethical awareness.

9.2 High-Risk AI Failure Modes in Bioinformatics
Large language models are probabilistic word prediction engines, not biological execution environments. In specialized scientific computing, they frequently fail in predictable ways:

Table 2: Common AI hazards in bioinformatics







Hazard
Mechanism
Biological Consequence




1. Flag Hallucination
Models invent plausible-sounding flags that do not exist
Pipeline crashes with unrecognized option or silently misbehaves


2. Deprecated Syntax & Tools
Trained on older web data (e.g. Biostars archives)
Recommends dead tools (TopHat2, Python 2) rather than modern standards


3. Biological Confabulation
Confabulates gene targets or cites fake literature
Claims non-existent SNPs cause drug resistance; cites fabricated PubMed DOIs


4. The Copy-Paste Blindspot
Learners bypass cognitive effort during training
Zero skill retention; completely helpless when the AI prompt fails



1. Flag Hallucinations: Mixing Tools
LLMs frequently merge options from competing tools. For example, when asked to write a BWA-MEM command, an AI might insert --local (a Bowtie2 flag) or --very-sensitive. In other cases, it will invent flags that sound intuitive (e.g. fastp --min-depth 20) but have never existed in the tool’s source code.
2. The Trap of Outdated Standards
Because training data contains vast amounts of legacy forum discussions from 2012–2018, models frequently suggest obsolete bioinformatics practices:

Recommending TopHat instead of HISAT2 or STAR.
Using deprecated GATK3 syntax (-T UnifiedGenotyper) instead of GATK4 (HaplotypeCaller).
Writing Python 2 scripts that fail on modern Linux operating systems.

section: 9.3 Data Privacy, Ethics, and Genomic Sovereignty
text:
9.3 Data Privacy, Ethics, and Genomic Sovereignty
Commercial cloud AI services (free and paid web chatbots) routinely log user prompts to refine future models.
Bioinformatics researchers must observe strict ethical and regulatory processes:






WarningThree Dont-dos for AI Prompts




Never Paste Patient Health Information: Never include patient names, hospital record numbers, geographic identifiers, or identifiable clinical metadata.
Never Paste Unconsented Raw Human DNA Sequences: Uploading human genomic reads or individual variant lists to commercial third-party cloud servers can violate national data protection laws (e.g. GDPR, national health ethics board approvals).
Never Expose Sensitive Pathogen Outbreak Data: Pasting unreleased genome assemblies of high-consequence pathogens (e.g. Ebola, Marburg, novel avian influenza) into public chatbots before national public health clearance violates public health reporting protocols and national genomic sovereignty.




9.3.1 Safe Alternatives for Sensitive Clinical Work:

Anonymized Synthetic Snippets: Replace real patient barcodes with sample_01, and use generic synthetic sequences (ATCG...).
Offline Local Open-Source Models: Run open-weights models (such as Llama 3 or Mistral) locally on institutional workstations using lightweight tools like Ollama. These run entirely in RAM with zero internet connection, guaranteeing 100% data sovereignty.

text:
9.7 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will test your ability to spot subtle AI errors and guide students toward responsible AI usage.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Spotting the Hallucination in AI-Generated Code






A trainee prompts an AI tool: “Write me a Bash command to filter variants in my bacterial VCF file using BCFtools, keeping only SNPs with depth over 20 and quality over 30.”
The AI returns:
bcftools filter --min-coverage 20 --min-quality 30 --type snp raw.vcf > filtered.vcf

Identify the three hallucinations in this command.
What error will BCFtools return when the trainee runs this?
Provide the correct, robust BCFtools command.







HintHint






Check the official bcftools filter syntax. Does BCFtools use double-dash long flags like --min-coverage, or does it use expression filters (-e / -i)?










AnswerAnswer






9.7.1 Hallucination Audit & Correction

Three Hallucinations:

--min-coverage 20: Does not exist in BCFtools filter (likely borrowed from GATK or VarScan). BCFtools uses the INFO/FORMAT tag DP.
--min-quality 30: Does not exist. BCFtools filters quality using the column tag QUAL.
--type snp: Does not exist in bcftools filter. Filtering by variant type is done via bcftools view -v snps or inside filter expressions with TYPE="snp".

Terminal Output: BCFtools will exit immediately with: [E::main] unrecognized option '--min-coverage'
Correct BCFtools Command:
bcftools filter -i 'QUAL >= 30 && DP >= 20 && TYPE="snp"' raw.vcf -o filtered.vcf















ExerciseExercise 2 - Guiding a Trainee Suffering from AI Dependency






During the afternoon practical, you notice that a master’s student has two windows open: the workshop tutorial and an AI chatbot. Every time an exercise appears, the student copies the prompt into the AI, copies the generated code, and pastes it into the terminal.
When you ask the student: “Why did you use the -S flag in that less command?”, the student hesitates and replies: “I don’t know, ChatGPT told me to put it there.”

What pedagogical harm is occurring here?
How would you intervene supportively without shaming the student?
What rule can you establish for the remainder of the session to restore active learning?







AnswerAnswer






9.7.2 Facilitator Intervention

Pedagogical Harm: The student is bypassing the active struggle necessary to build long-term neural pathways and spatial mental models. By using AI as an intellectual crutch, the student gains an illusion of competence while remaining completely incapable of debugging or modifying pipelines independently.
Supportive Intervention:

Acknowledge that using modern tools is understandable: “I see you are using AI to help with syntax—in research, AI can be a great accelerator!”
Highlight the gap: “However, when you return to your laboratory, the AI won’t be able to tell you why your thesis data failed if you don’t understand what these flags mean.”
Demystify the flag collaboratively: “Let’s test what happens if you run less with and without -S right now on your screen. Do you see how -S stops the lines from wrapping? Now you own that knowledge, not the chatbot!”

Actionable Rule: Implement the “Explain Before Run” Rule: “You may use AI to give you hints, but before you hit Enter on any command, you must be able to turn to your partner and explain what every single flag does. If you can’t explain it, you can’t run it!”

TipKey Points




AI is an Accelerator, Not a Substitute: Large language models act as invaluable 24/7 mentors for isolated researchers in low-resource settings, but they cannot replace foundational computational understanding.
Expect Hallucinations: AI models frequently invent non-existent tool flags, suggest obsolete software pipelines, and confuse competing syntax.
Follow the “Trust but Verify” Protocol: Always verify AI flags against official binary help pages (tool --help) and execute dry runs on micro-datasets before scaling up.
Maintain Ethical Red Lines: Never upload unconsented patient health information, identifiable human DNA sequences, or restricted pathogen genomic data to commercial cloud AI chatbots.
Enforce Context-Rich Prompting: Provide specific software versions, exact error traces, and input/output formats to receive accurate technical assistance.
Implement Clear Classroom Policies: Encourage AI for explaining error messages and commenting code, but restrict it during foundational mental-model construction.

text:
10.1 Introduction: Why Reinvent the Wheel?
Creating a modern, high-quality bioinformatics curriculum from scratch requires hundreds of hours of design, code testing, dataset curating, and slide preparation. For educators in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), who frequently balance heavy university teaching loads, clinical duties, wet-lab management, and administrative responsibilities, building an entire curriculum from the ground up is an overwhelming burden.
Fortunately, the global scientific community has embraced Open Educational Resources (OER). Today, thousands of peer-reviewed, classroom-tested bioinformatics lessons, interactive workflows, and curated datasets are freely available online.
The role of a modern bioinformatics educator in a resource-limited setting is not to author every line of training material from scratch. Your aim is curating, contextualizing, and delivering existing open resources to meet the precise needs of your local learners.

section: 10.2 What Are Open Educational Resources? The 5Rs
text:
10.2 What Are Open Educational Resources? The 5Rs
According to UNESCO, Open Educational Resources (OER) are learning, teaching, and research materials in any format and medium that reside in the public domain or are released under an open license that permits no-cost access, reuse, repurpose, adaptation, and redistribution by others.
Educational researcher David Wiley codified the operational definition of open content into the “5R Permissions”:



The five R’s of Open Educational Resources (OER)



Retain: The right to make, own, and control copies of the content (e.g. downloading lessons to offline USB drives without fear of expiration or paywalls).
Reuse: The right to use the content in its original, unaltered form (e.g. running a Software Carpentry Unix tutorial in your workshop).
Revise: The right to adapt, adjust, modify, or translate the content (e.g. replacing a human cancer dataset with local Plasmodium falciparum sequencing data).
Remix: The right to combine the original or revised content with other open materials to create something new (e.g. merging a Galaxy QC tutorial with an R visualization practical).
Redistribute: The right to share copies of your original, revised, or remixed materials with your students, regional colleagues, and the public.

10.3 The FAIR Principles for Training Materials
Just as research data must be FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable), international bioinformatics training networks (including ELIXIR and the Global Bioinformatics Education Network) have established the FAIR Principles for Training Materials:

Table 2: FAIR principles in bioinformatics training






Principle
Practical Implementation for Instructors




1. Findable
• Deposit materials in indexed registries (TeSS)• Assign persistent identifiers (DOIs via Zenodo)• Include structured metadata (keywords, targets)


2. Accessible
• Publish on open, barrier-free platforms (web)• Guarantee clear access protocols (no paywalls)• Provide downloadable offline copies (PDF/HTML)


3. Interoperable
• Use open, plain-text formats (Markdown, Quarto)• Reference standard biological ontologies (EDAM)• Avoid proprietary vendor-locked slide formats


4. Reusable
• Attach an explicit open license (e.g. CC BY)• Define prerequisites & target learner personas• Provide executable code & micro-datasets



Adopting FAIR training practices ensures that your localized materials don’t disappear on an abandoned hard drive when a grant concludes, but remain findable and reusable by educators worldwide.

text:
10.4 Open Licensing: Navigating Creative Commons
A common misconception is that anything freely accessible on the internet is open to be copied, modified, and redistributed. Under international copyright law, works without an explicit license are protected by “All Rights Reserved” by default.
To grant the 5R permissions, authors attach Creative Commons (CC) licenses:

Table 3: Creative commons licensing spectrum








License
Requirements
Is it OER?
Impact on Teaching




CC0 (No Rights)
Public Domain (No attribution)
Yes (Full)
Unconditional reuse


CC BY
Attribution only
Yes (Gold Standard)
Ideal for science; free to adapt/remix


CC BY-SA
Attribution + ShareAlike
Yes
Derived works must keep the same license


CC BY-NC
Attribution + NonCommercial
Yes (With Caveat)
Cannot be used in fee-charging courses


CC BY-ND
Attribution + NoDerivatives
❌ NO! (Not OER)
Cannot adapt, modify, or translate files!









WarningThe “NoDerivatives” Trap (CC BY-ND)



Materials licensed under CC BY-ND prohibit any modification or derivative works. You can show the material in its exact original state, but you cannot translate it into French or Swahili, simplify the text, or swap out the example dataset for a local pathogen. For true educational adaptation, always look for CC BY or CC BY-SA materials.



10.4.1 How to Give Proper Attribution (The TASL Principle)
When using or adapting OER content, follow the TASL framework:

Title: What is the name of the resource?
Author: Who created it?
Source: Where did you find it (link to repository)?
License: Under which CC license is it released (link to license)?

Example Citation:

“Adapted from ‘Introduction to the Command Line for Genomics’ by The Carpentries, licensed under CC BY 4.0. Regional malaria datasets substituted by Dr. A. Mensah.”

10.6 Adapting OER for LMICs
Simply downloading an open curriculum created at a well-funded European or North American university and presenting it unaltered to an LMIC classroom often leads to failure.
Curricula from high-resource settings frequently embed hidden resource assumptions:

“Download this 15 GB reference file from NCBI during class.” (Classroom Wi-Fi collapses).
“Run this Nextflow pipeline across 32 cores on your institutional cluster.” (Students only have 4 GB RAM laptops).
“Let us explore mutations associated with cystic fibrosis in European populations.” (Completely divorced from the infectious disease or agricultural priorities of local trainees).




The contextualisation process








NoteThe Power of Local Biological Relevance



Adult learners are motivated by immediate practical relevance (Knowles’ andragogical principle). When you teach variant calling using a local multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolate or a drought-resistant local cowpea variety, learner engagement increases dramatically compared to analyzing human cancer cell line datasets.

text:
10.9 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will test your ability to evaluate licenses, audit training materials for hidden resource barriers, and adapt generic lessons to local realities.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Evaluating Open Licenses for Workshop Use






You are organizing a 5 day regional bioinformatics workshop in East Africa. To cover venue rental, coffee breaks, and printed materials, your university charges participants a nominal registration fee of $30 USD.
You identify three online tutorials you would like to adapt and bundle into the course manual:

Tutorial A: Marked “Copyright © 2024 University X. All Rights Reserved.”
Tutorial B: Licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (Attribution-NonCommercial).
Tutorial C: Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 (Attribution-ShareAlike).


Can you legally download, modify, and print Tutorial A for your participants?
Does charging a $30 cost-recovery registration fee violate the non-commercial restriction of Tutorial B?
What legal obligation do you have if you adapt Tutorial C and distribute the revised manual to your students?







HintHint






Review the legal distinction between commercial exploitation and non-profit cost-recovery, and remember the “ShareAlike” clause.










AnswerAnswer






10.9.1 Legal & Licensing Evaluation

Tutorial A (All Rights Reserved): No. Without an explicit open license, international copyright law prohibits unauthorized copying, modification, or redistribution, even for non-profit education. You must contact the original authors to obtain written permission.
Tutorial B (CC BY-NC 4.0): High legal ambiguity / Risk. Creative Commons defines non-commercial as “not primarily intended for or directed towards commercial advantage or monetary compensation”. While charging a nominal registration fee to cover catering/venue costs is considered cost-recovery by educators, some institutional legal teams interpret any fee as commercial. If possible, seek clarification from the author or choose a pure CC BY resource to avoid legal ambiguity.
Tutorial C (CC BY-SA 4.0): Yes, you can freely use, adapt, and print it. However, under the ShareAlike (SA) clause, your adapted manual must also be released under the exact same CC BY-SA 4.0 license, and you must provide proper attribution (TASL) to the original creators.















ExerciseExercise 2 - Auditing and Contextualizing a High-resource Setting OER Lesson






You find a popular, well-written online tutorial on “RNA-Seq Differential Expression Analysis” published by an institute in the United States.
The original lesson:

Downloads a 12 GB paired-end mouse dataset from the NCBI SRA via fastq-dump during class.
Uses STAR aligner (requiring 32 GB of RAM to build the genome index).
Explores gene expression changes in mouse liver tissue following high-fat diet consumption.

Audit this lesson and describe three concrete modifications you must make to adapt it for a classroom of 20 trainees in Ghana with 8 GB RAM laptops and a 5 Mbps shared Wi-Fi connection.






AnswerAnswer






10.9.2 Adaptation Audit & Redesign

Bandwidth Remediation:

Problem: Running fastq-dump across 20 laptops for 12 GB will crash the 5 Mbps network within minutes.
Fix: Subsample the raw reads into a micro-dataset beforehand. Distribute the subsampled FASTQ files via USB flash drives or a local classroom router so zero internet bandwidth is required.

Hardware Remediation:

Problem: STAR requires 32 GB RAM just to load the mammalian genome index, which will immediately trigger an Out-Of-Memory (Killed) crash on 8 GB student laptops.
Fix: Replace STAR with a lightweight pseudo-aligner (such as kallisto or salmon), which runs in under 2 GB of RAM and executes in minutes, OR use a single-chromosome/micro-dataset index.

Biological Contextualization:

Problem: Mouse liver metabolic response to high-fat diets is irrelevant to local public health and infectious disease research in Ghana.
Fix: Swap the dataset for an authentic public dataset investigating transcriptional responses of Plasmodium falciparum to artemisinin treatment, or a local crop (cassava mosaic virus resistance). The core statistical principles (counts, normalisation, DESeq2, Volcano plots, FDR) remain 100% identical, but learner motivation and local relevance are dramatically enhanced.

TipKey Points




Leverage Existing OER: Avoid curriculum burnout by adapting previously tested, peer-reviewed educational materials from global communities rather than writing courses from scratch.
The 5Rs Define Openness: True OER grants the rights to Retain, Reuse, Revise, Remix, and Redistribute content freely.
Adopt FAIR Training Principles: Ensure training materials are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable by using open formats (Markdown/Quarto), attaching DOIs, and providing clear metadata.
Choose the Right License: Favor CC BY (Attribution) for maximum educational flexibility; avoid CC BY-ND (NoDerivatives), which legally prohibits adapting or translating materials.
Contextualization is Mandatory: Never deliver curricula from high-resources settings unexamined. Proactively strip bandwidth-heavy live downloads, right-size compute requirements for modest hardware, and replace generic model organisms with regionally relevant health and agricultural datasets.
Plan for Offline Delivery: Mirror websites (wget --mirror), package static HTML books, and distribute micro-datasets on USB flash drives to insulate courses from internet outages.

title: 11  Containerisation
text:
11.1 Introduction: “It Works on My Machine”
Bioinformatics tools have notoriously intricate dependency chains. A single phylogenetics or metagenomics pipeline might require a specific version of Python, an outdated Perl module, particular C++ compiler libraries (glibc), and dozens of specialized R packages.
In a traditional workshop setting, instructors often spend the entire first day walking around the room diagnosing failed installations across different student operating systems (Windows 10, Windows 11, macOS Intel, macOS Apple Silicon, and assorted Linux distributions). This scenario, known as “dependency hell”, wastes valuable instructional time and demoralizes novice learners.
Containerisation solves this fundamental challenge. It allows developers and trainers to package an entire software environment, including the operating system, tools, libraries, dependencies, and configuration files, into a single, portable, self-contained unit that runs identically on any computer.

title: 11  Containerisation
section: 11.2 The Conceptual Model: Containers vs Virtual Machines
text:
11.2 The Conceptual Model: Containers vs Virtual Machines
To teach containers effectively, instructors must first address the question every computational novice asks: “Isn’t this just a Virtual Machine?”. To answer this question you must first understand the differences yourself.
The physical shipping container analogy remains the most powerful mental model:






NoteThe Intermodal Shipping Container Analogy



Before the 1950s, cargo was loaded loosely onto ships as “break bulk”, sacks of grain, barrels of oil, and wooden crates of varying sizes. Loading a ship was slow, labor-intensive, and prone to damage. The invention of the standardized intermodal shipping container revolutionized global commerce: cranes, trucks, trains, and cargo ships now handle the exact same steel box regardless of whether it holds bananas, medical devices, or cars.
Software containers are the standardized shipping boxes of computing. The host operating system doesn’t need to know what specific libraries or Python versions are inside; it simply runs the container.





Virtual machines versus containers



11.2.1 Key Differences Every Trainer Should Know

Table 1: Differences between virtual machines and software containers







Feature
Virtual Machine (VM)
Software Container




Architecture
Virtualises physical hardware; runs a complete guest operating system kernel.
Shares the host OS kernel; isolates processes and user libraries.


Startup Time
Slow (minutes to boot the guest OS).
Instantaneous (sub-second process launch).


Resource Overhead
High: allocates fixed RAM and CPU cores (e.g. reserving 4 GB RAM away from host).
Minimal: consumes only the exact memory and CPU used by the running process.


Performance
Significant performance penalty for disk I/O and computation.
Near-native bare-metal execution speed.


Low-Resource Suitability
Poor for 4–8 GB RAM laptops (causes heavy swapping).
Excellent: low footprint allows running on modest hardware.

title: 11  Containerisation
text:
11.3 Docker vs Singularity / Apptainer
The container landscape in science is dominated by two primary technologies: Docker and Singularity (now largely standardized and maintained under the Linux Foundation as Apptainer).
Understanding their architectural differences is vital, especially when training researchers who move between personal laptops and institutional HPC clusters.

Table 2: Docker versus Singularity/Apptainer






Docker
Singularity/Apptainer




• Native to industry & cloud
• Native to academic HPC & science


• Requires background daemon
• No background daemon needed


• Requires root / sudo access (Security risk on shared HPC)
• Runs entirely as unprivileged user (Safe on multi-user HPC)


• Container filesystems isolated by default (must bind manually)
• Mounts user’s home and current directory by default


• Multi-layered image storage
• Stored as a single standalone file (.sif) – easy to copy!




11.3.1 Why Singularity / Apptainer is the Scientific Standard

Security & Permissions: Docker requires root privileges or membership in the docker user group (which is functionally equivalent to root access). On shared university servers or national HPC facilities, system administrators strictly prohibit Docker. Apptainer runs with whatever permissions the logged-in user possesses—if you cannot edit /etc/shadow on the host, you cannot edit it inside the container.
Single-File Portability (.sif): Singularity encapsulates the entire container environment into a single Singularity Image File (.sif). You can copy this file like a regular document via a USB flash drive or scp, making it ideal for offline distribution in low-resource settings.
Seamless Filesystem Integration: By default, Apptainer automatically mounts the user’s current directory ($PWD) and home directory ($HOME), making running a container feel like executing a local command.

title: 11  Containerisation
text:
11.4 Hands-on Container Operations
1. Working with Docker
When teaching on personal machines or cloud virtual machines (where users have root access), Docker is straightforward:
# Pull a container from Docker Hub
docker pull biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1

# Run fastp inside the container
docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)/data":/data \
  biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1 \
  fastp -i /data/sample_R1.fq.gz -I /data/sample_R2.fq.gz -o /data/clean_R1.fq.gz -O /data/clean_R2.fq.gz






ImportantDemystifying Volume Mounting (-v)



The most common mistake beginners make with Docker is forgetting that the container is isolated from the host laptop. If you run:
docker run biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1 fastp -i sample_R1.fq.gz
Docker will immediately abort with Cannot find input file: sample_R1.fq.gz.
The Window Metaphor: volume mounting (-v /local/path:/container/path) is like cutting a transparent window between their personal laptop and the sealed shipping container. Without that window, the tool inside cannot reach outside to see the data, and any output produced will vanish when the container exits!


2. Working with Singularity / Apptainer
Apptainer can convert and run any existing Docker image directly without requiring Docker to be installed:
# Build / convert a Docker image into a single .sif file
apptainer build fastp.sif docker://biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1

# Execute a tool directly using the .sif container
apptainer exec fastp.sif fastp --help

# Run a complete command (current directory is automatically mounted!)
apptainer exec fastp.sif fastp \
  -i sample_R1.fq.gz -I sample_R2.fq.gz \
  -o clean_R1.fq.gz -O clean_R2.fq.gz \
  --html fastp_report.html
Notice how much simpler this is: there is no complex volume mounting syntax needed for files located in the current working directory!

title: 11  Containerisation
text:
11.6 Container Strategies for Low-Resource Environments
While containers solve software installation hurdles, they introduce a major bottleneck in low-resource environments: bandwidth consumption.
A typical bioinformatics container ranges from 500 MB to 3 GB in size. If 25 workshop participants simultaneously run docker pull or apptainer pull over a shared 10 Mbps classroom connection:

The network connection will collapse immediately.
Trainees will face timeout errors, partial downloads, and high mobile data bills.




Classroom bandwidth collapse



11.6.1 Practical Offline Distribution Workflows
Strategy 1: The “Sneakernet” USB Stick Distribution (Recommended)
Trainers download and package all required containers onto high-speed USB flash drives prior to arriving at the venue.

For Docker:
# On instructor's machine (before the course):
docker pull biocontainers/bwa:v0.7.17_cv1
docker save biocontainers/bwa:v0.7.17_cv1 -o bwa_image.tar

# On student's machine (during the course from USB):
docker load -i /media/usb/bwa_image.tar
For Singularity / Apptainer:
# On instructor's machine:
apptainer build bwa.sif docker://biocontainers/bwa:v0.7.17_cv1

# Simply copy bwa.sif directly from the USB drive to the student's laptop!
cp /media/usb/bwa.sif ~/course_tools/

Strategy 2: Local Classroom Wi-Fi Cache / Mini-Registry
If students have decent local connectivity to a local router (even without an active internet gateway):

The instructor sets up a local Docker registry or simple HTTP server (e.g. python3 -m http.server 8000) on a laptop or Raspberry Pi connected to the classroom Wi-Fi router.
Students download .sif files or pull images locally at 100–300 Mbps over local Wi-Fi without consuming any cellular or external internet bandwidth.

title: 11  Containerisation
text:
11.7 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will help you anticipate common student hurdles and plan resilient containerised training sessions.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Diagnosing Disappearing Results






During a hands-on sequencing analysis practical, a student runs read trimming using Docker on their laptop:
docker run --rm biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1 \
  fastp -i /data/raw_R1.fq.gz -o /data/trimmed_R1.fq.gz
The tool runs to completion, printing:
Read 1 before filtering: 500000 reads
Read 1 after filtering: 489120 reads
Trimming completed successfully.
The student returns to their terminal prompt and types ls. The file trimmed_R1.fq.gz is nowhere to be found. In panic, the student asks: “It said it finished successfully, but where did my data go?”

What caused the output file to disappear?
What role did the --rm flag play in this scenario?
How would you explain this concept to the student, and what is the corrected command?







HintHint






Consider where /data/trimmed_R1.fq.gz was written and whether that directory exists on the host laptop or only inside the container.










AnswerAnswer






11.7.1 Explanation & Resolution

Cause: The student failed to mount a local host directory using the -v flag. The file trimmed_R1.fq.gz was written to /data/ inside the container’s isolated, ephemeral filesystem.
Role of --rm: The --rm flag instructs Docker to immediately delete the container’s writeable layer when the process exits. Because the container was destroyed upon exit and had no mounted host volume, the generated file was permanently deleted.
Trainer Explanation & Corrected Command: “Think of the container as a clean, disposable laboratory bench in another building. You ran the experiment inside that building, but you forgot to open a window to pass the tubes back into your office. When the experiment finished, the cleaning crew wiped the bench clean.”
Corrected Command:
docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)":/data \
  biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1 \
  fastp -i /data/raw_R1.fq.gz -o /data/trimmed_R1.fq.gz















ExerciseExercise 2 - Planning an Offline Training Session






You are invited to lead a 3 day bacterial genomics workshop at a regional university in an area known for frequent internet throttling and power cuts. The course requires three tools: fastp, spades, and prokka.

Why should you avoid asking participants to install these tools during the first morning of class?
Which container engine (Docker or Apptainer) would you recommend if the students are using shared institutional Linux workstations, and why?
Outline your step-by-step preparation protocol before traveling to the workshop venue to guarantee that zero internet bandwidth will be required for software access.







AnswerAnswer






11.7.2 Strategic Workshop Plan

Avoid Live Installs: Downloading Conda environments or container layers for 25–30 students simultaneously would require over 40 GB of network traffic. In an unstable network, packages will fail mid-download, checksums will fail, and day one will be lost to debugging.
Engine Recommendation: Apptainer (Singularity). Institutional shared workstations rarely grant individual participants sudo or root privileges. Docker cannot run without root access, whereas Apptainer runs securely in user space.
Pre-Course Preparation Protocol:

Step 1 (Pre-build): On the trainer’s high-speed home network, build standalone .sif files for all three tools from BioContainers:
apptainer build fastp.sif docker://quay.io/biocontainers/fastp:v0.23.4_cv1
apptainer build spades.sif docker://quay.io/biocontainers/spades:3.15.5--h95f258a_1
apptainer build prokka.sif docker://quay.io/biocontainers/prokka:1.14.6--pl5321hdfd78af_5
Step 2 (Package): Copy fastp.sif, spades.sif, prokka.sif, and the subsampled micro-datasets onto 5–10 fast USB 3.0 flash drives.
Step 3 (Distribute): On the first morning, circulate the USB drives. Students copy the .sif files into a ~/tools/ folder in under 2 minutes per laptop.
Result: Complete independence from internet availability throughout the workshop.

11.8 Summary






TipKey Points




Containers Guarantee Parity: Containers encapsulate application code, dependencies, and system libraries, eliminating the “works on my machine” barrier and saving hours of classroom troubleshooting.
Lightweight vs Virtual Machines: Containers share the host operating system kernel, making them fast to launch and resource-efficient enough to run on modest 4–8 GB RAM laptops.
Docker for Personal/Cloud, Apptainer for HPC: Docker requires root access and a background daemon; Singularity/Apptainer runs unprivileged, mounts user directories automatically, and packages environments into single .sif files suitable for shared academic clusters.
Isolation Requires Volume Mounting: In Docker, data is ephemeral unless explicit volumes (-v) connect host paths to container paths.

title: 12  Software Installation
section: 12.2 How the Operating System Finds Software: Demystifying $PATH
text:
12.2 How the Operating System Finds Software: Demystifying $PATH
Before understanding package managers, you must understand how the operating system executes a command. You may frequently encounter the error command not found and assume the installation failed, when in reality the executable simply resides in an unindexed folder.

12.2.1 The $PATH Environment Variable
When a user types fastp and hits Enter, the operating system does not search the entire computer. Instead, it consults an environment variable called $PATH, a colon-separated list of directories where executable programs reside.
User types: fastp
     │
     ▼
Consult $PATH:  /usr/local/bin : /usr/bin : /bin : /home/user/.local/bin
                      │              │        │               │
                      ▼              ▼        ▼               ▼
                 Check here     Check here  Found!        (Skipped)
                 (Not found)    (Not found) [Execute]
To see which directories are currently searched:
echo "$PATH"
To determine which specific binary is being executed:
which fastp
# or
type -a fastp


12.2.2 Making a Program Executable: Permissions
In Unix, a downloaded file cannot run simply because it has a particular extension. It must have the executable (x) permission bit set:
# Check file permissions
ls -l my_script.sh
# -rw-r--r-- 1 trainee trainee 1024 Oct 1 09:00 my_script.sh (Cannot run!)

# Grant execute permission
chmod +x my_script.sh

# Now it can run
ls -l my_script.sh
# -rwxr-xr-x 1 trainee trainee 1024 Oct 1 09:01 my_script.sh (Executable!)






NoteThe . in ./program



Beginners often ask: “Why do I have to type ./fastp when I am inside the folder containing fastp, but I can type ls from anywhere?”

ls lives in /bin, which is listed in $PATH.
For security reasons, the current working directory (.) is almost never included in $PATH.
Typing ./program explicitly instructs the shell: “Look right here in the current folder (.) and execute program.”

12.4 Static and Pre-Compiled Binaries
A statically linked binary has all of its supporting libraries compiled directly into a single executable file. It has no external dependencies.

Examples: seqkit, minimap2, fastp, samtools (standalone releases).
Why they excel in low-resource settings:

Zero dependencies: no Python, Perl, or Conda required.
Extremely small download footprint (typically 5 MB – 25 MB).
Can be downloaded once, placed onto a USB drive, copied into any user’s ~/.local/bin/ folder, and executed immediately.

section: 12.5 Modern Package Management: Conda, Mamba, and Micromamba
text:
12.5 Modern Package Management: Conda, Mamba, and Micromamba
For software with complex multi-language dependencies, package managers are essential. In bioinformatics, the Conda ecosystem (specifically the Bioconda and Conda-forge channels) is the standard.



The conda ecoystem



12.5.1 Why Classic Conda Fails on Low-Resource Hardware
Classic conda was written in Python and uses a Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) solver to resolve dependencies. As the Bioconda repository grew to tens of thousands of packages, solving an environment became computationally intensive:

Classic Conda often requires 2.5 GB to 4 GB of RAM just to calculate the dependency graph.
On an older 4 GB RAM student laptop, the OS runs out of memory, triggers disk swapping, and kills the process with Killed or hangs indefinitely (“Solving environment: ").



12.5.2 The Solution: Mamba and Micromamba
Mamba replaces Conda’s Python solver with a high-performance C++ solver (libsolv), reducing solve times from 20 minutes to 15 seconds while consuming a fraction of the RAM.
Micromamba goes one step further: it is a single, self-contained C++ executable (~10 MB) that requires no existing Python installation and can create complete bioinformatics environments from scratch.






TipBest Practice: Always Use Micromamba / Mamba



When dealing with package management in low-resource workshops, always recommend Mamba or Miniforge instead of the bloated Anaconda Distribution (which installs over 5 GB of unneeded data science libraries).




12.5.3 Never Install Software into the Base Environment
One of the most software related issues that arises in bioinformatics is a corrupted base environment.
Never install research tools into the base environment. Always create dedicated, isolated environments for distinct projects:
# Create a dedicated environment for bacterial genome assembly
mamba create -n assembly_env -c conda-forge -c biococonda \
  spades fastp quast

# Activate the environment
mamba activate assembly_env

# Check which environments exist
mamba env list

# Deactivate when finished
mamba deactivate

title: 12  Software Installation
text:
12.6 Managing Python and R Dependencies
Bioinformaticians frequently work with custom Python and R scripts that require community libraries.

12.6.1 1. Python Environments
Never install packages globally using sudo pip install. Instead:

Use Python’s built-in virtual environment module:
python3 -m venv my_project_env
source my_project_env/bin/activate
pip install pandas biopython matplotlib
Modern Alternative: In resource-constrained environments, tools like uv (written in Rust) install Python wheels 10–50 times faster than pip and manage local Python versions with minimal disk footprint.



12.6.2 2. R Packages and Bioconductor
R packages in bioinformatics are split between CRAN and Bioconductor:
# Installing BiocManager and genomic packages
if (!require("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("DESeq2")






WarningHidden C Libraries and R



Many R bioinformatics packages (e.g. DESeq2, RCurl, xml2) are wrappers around underlying C/C++ libraries. Installing them from source in R on a clean Linux machine will fail if system libraries like libxml2-dev, libcurl4-openssl-dev, or libssl-dev are missing.
Trainer Advice: If students are working on Linux or WSL, prefer installing R packages via Conda/Mamba (mamba install r-deseq2), which installs the underlying compiled system libraries automatically without requiring root permissions.

12.7 Strategies for Low-Bandwidth and Offline Workflows
How can instructors deliver a hands-on workshop when the classroom internet is unreliable or completely absent?



Offline conda packing workflow



12.7.1 1. conda-pack: Transporting Pre-Built Environments
conda-pack is an open-source tool that archives an existing Conda environment into a .tar.gz file. - It preserves all compiled binaries, dependencies, and path prefixes. - Students unpack the archive into their local envs/ directory and activate it immediately. - Advantage: Bypasses all package index downloads, dependency resolution, and compilation.


12.7.2 2. Standalone Binary Bundles
For courses focusing on standard sequencing pipelines (QC, mapping, variant calling), create a single zipped folder containing pre-compiled static Linux/macOS binaries (fastp, samtools, minimap2, bedtools). Students unzip the folder and add it to their $PATH in one command:
unzip course_binaries.zip -d ~/
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/course_binaries:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

text:
12.8 Pedagogical Guidelines: Zero-Downtime Installation

12.8.1 1. The Pre-Course Installation Clinic
Never schedule installation as the opening lecture on Day 1. Instead:

Host a drop-in virtual “Installation Clinic” 2–3 days prior to the course.
Assign teaching assistants or workshop helpers to test student machines one-on-one.
If a student cannot resolve their issues before Day 1, transition them to a pre-configured backup option (e.g. a cloud instance, web-based platform, or loaner USB with pre-packaged binaries).



12.8.2 2. Automated Pre-Flight Verification Scripts
Provide learners with a simple, self-contained shell script that checks whether all required tools are correctly installed and functional before the course begins:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ==============================================================================
# preflight_check.sh: Verifies required workshop tools
# ==============================================================================

echo "Checking workshop tools..."
TOOLS=("fastp" "bwa" "samtools" "spades" "python3")
MISSING=0

for tool in "${TOOLS[@]}"; do
    if command -v "${tool}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "  [OK] ${tool} is installed: $(which ${tool})"
    else
        echo "  [FAIL] ${tool} is NOT found in your \$PATH!"
        MISSING=$((MISSING + 1))
    fi
done

if [ ${MISSING} -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "SUCCESS: All tools verified! You are ready for the workshop."
else
    echo "WARNING: ${MISSING} tool(s) missing. Please contact a trainer."
fi

title: 12  Software Installation
text:
12.9 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will challenge you to troubleshoot real-world installation failures and plan resilient teaching workflows.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Diagnosing “Command Not Found”






During a morning practical, a student downloads the static binary for seqkit from GitHub. They place it in their home directory ~/Downloads/. In their terminal, they type:
$ cd ~/projects/malaria/
$ seqkit stats sample.fasta
bash: seqkit: command not found
In distress, the student raises their hand: “I downloaded seqkit, but my computer says it isn’t there! Did the download fail?”

What are the two distinct computational reasons why this command failed?
How would you guide the student to diagnose and fix the problem using terminal commands?
What long-term configuration step should you teach the student so they can execute seqkit from any directory in the future?







HintHint






Check whether the directory containing seqkit is in the user’s $PATH, and whether the downloaded file has execute permissions.










AnswerAnswer






12.9.1 Diagnosis & Remediation

Root Causes:

Path Disconnect: The binary is in ~/Downloads/, but ~/Downloads/ is not in $PATH. When the user is in ~/projects/malaria/, the shell cannot find it.
Missing Permissions: Freshly downloaded files from web browsers typically lack the executable bit (x).

Diagnosis & Immediate Fix:
# Check if file exists and inspect permissions
ls -l ~/Downloads/seqkit

# Grant execute permission
chmod +x ~/Downloads/seqkit

# Run with explicit path
~/Downloads/seqkit stats sample.fasta
Permanent Solution: Move the binary to a standard user directory that is already in $PATH (or add a custom directory to $PATH in .bashrc):
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
mv ~/Downloads/seqkit ~/.local/bin/
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc















ExerciseExercise 2 - Selecting the Best Installation Strategy






You are designing a 4 day metagenomics workshop for 20 master’s students at an institute in East Africa. The institutional computer lab has 10 desktop machines running an old version of Ubuntu Linux without internet access. Students will bring 10 personal Windows laptops connected to an unstable 4 Mbps shared mobile Wi-Fi hotspot.
The course requires fastp, megahit, and kraken2 (with an 8 GB mini-database).
For each of the two groups (Lab Desktops vs. Personal Windows Laptops), select the most robust installation and distribution strategy. Justify your choices based on internet bandwidth, administrative permissions, and hardware constraints.






AnswerAnswer






12.9.2 Strategic Deployment Plan

For the Lab Linux Desktops (No Internet, Unknown Root Access):

Strategy: Standalone .sif container images via Apptainer or pre-packed Conda archives via conda-pack, distributed via USB flash drives.
Justification: Because there is zero internet access, network-based package managers are impossible. Apptainer .sif files or unpacked conda-pack folders run entirely offline without requiring root access or internet connectivity. The 8 GB Kraken2 database can be copied directly to local /scratch or /data partitions from the same USB drive.

For Personal Windows Laptops (Unstable 4 Mbps Hotspot):

Strategy: Provide a pre-configured WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux) environment or lightweight Linux live USB drives pre-loaded with the software, OR distribute conda-pack archives for Windows/WSL via USB.
Justification: Attempting to have 10 Windows laptops download Conda environments and the 8 GB Kraken2 database over a shared 4 Mbps hotspot will take days and exhaust data quotas. Delivering all tools and the database offline via USB flash drives eliminates bandwidth dependency entirely.

12.10 Summary






TipKey Points




The $PATH Variable Controls Execution: The operating system searches only directories listed in $PATH. Understanding paths and the executable bit (chmod +x) resolves the vast majority of “command not found” errors.
Prefer Mamba/Micromamba Over Classic Conda: Classic Conda is prone to memory exhaustion (OOM crashes) on 4 GB–8 GB laptops due to its heavy Python solver. Mamba and Micromamba solve environments rapidly with minimal RAM.
Isolate Project Environments: Never install research tools directly into the base Conda environment.
Static Binaries are Low-Resource Allies: Standalone compiled binaries (e.g. fastp, seqkit) have zero dependencies, tiny download footprints, and can be circulated offline via USB.
Bypass Classroom Bandwidth with Offline Packaging: Tools like conda-pack and pre-built container images allow trainers to distribute complete, complex pipelines on USB flash drives without consuming a single megabyte of classroom internet.
Never Waste Day One on Installation: Run pre-course virtual installation clinics and provide automated pre-flight check scripts to ensure learners are ready to analyze data from minute one.

title: 13  Cloud-based Bioinformatics
text:
13.1 Introduction: Using Cloud Computing in Resource-Limited Settings
In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), establishing and maintaining a traditional institutional high-performance computing (HPC) cluster is prohibitively challenging. Hardware procurement involves heavy import tariffs, maintenance requires specialized system administrators, and unconditioned server rooms are vulnerable to electrical brownouts, power spikes, and air-conditioning failures.
Cloud computing transforms computational infrastructure from physical property into an on-demand utility. Instead of purchasing a $50,000 server that sits underutilized or overheats during power outages, researchers can rent virtual machines with 64 CPU cores and 256 GB of RAM for only the specific hours needed to run an assembly or variant-calling pipeline.
However, cloud computing is not necessarily the answer to all your computational research problems. For researchers in low-resource environments, the cloud introduces new, non-trivial challenges: financial barriers, international currency restrictions, high upload latencies, and data sovereignty considerations.

13.2 The Three Clouds: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS in Bioinformatics
When discussing “the cloud,” it’s important to understand the different service models. Understanding these models clarifies what technical skills are required:



The cloud service pyramid


1. Software as a Service (SaaS): Free Platforms like Galaxy

Galaxy (usegalaxy.org, usegalaxy.eu, usegalaxy.org.au): A web-based scientific analysis platform that provides thousands of bioinformatics tools behind a point-and-click GUI.
Why it matters for training: It is completely free for academic users, provides generous storage and compute quotas, requires zero command-line knowledge, and eliminates all local installation hurdles. Learners can run complex RNA-seq or variant calling workflows from a basic mobile browser or low-spec laptop.

2. Platform as a Service (PaaS): Interactive Notebooks & Portals

Google Colab & Kaggle Kernels: Provide free, cloud-hosted Jupyter Notebook environments with access to free GPUs (NVIDIA T4s) and TPUs. They are ideal for teaching Python-based data science, machine learning in genomics, or structural biology tools like ColabFold.
Biomedical Cloud Portals (Terra.bio, AnVIL): Managed platforms designed specifically for genomic research, hosting massive public datasets alongside standardized workflow execution engines (e.g. WDL/Nextflow).

3. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): Raw Compute Instances

Commercial Providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure): Users launch raw virtual machines (e.g. Amazon EC2, Google Compute Engine) running Ubuntu Linux.
Full Autonomy: The user has full root access to install any software, run custom pipelines, and configure CPU/RAM allocations freely.

text:
13.3 The Low-Resource Realities of Cloud Computing
While cloud infrastructure eliminates local hardware maintenance, instructors teaching in or from low-resource regions must proactively address four systemic challenges:
1. The Bandwidth Bottleneck: Upload vs. Download Asymmetry
In many LMICs, internet connections are highly asymmetric: download speeds might reach 10–20 Mbps, while upload speeds hover around 1–2 Mbps or suffer high packet loss.

Uploading a 50 GB paired-end sequencing run from a local lab to an AWS S3 bucket over a 2 Mbps connection will take more than 55 hours of uninterrupted connectivity—an impossibility in areas with daily power shedding.
The Solution: Data Locality (see below).

2. Financial Friction and Currency Controls
Commercial cloud providers require billing via credit cards in US Dollars, Euros, or British Pounds.

Many public universities in developing nations lack institutional credit cards.
Strict national foreign currency restrictions or severe inflation can make international card payments difficult or unpredictable.
The Solution: Academic credit grants (e.g. AWS Cloud Credit for Research, Google Cloud Research Grants) and centralized institutional vouchers.

3. “Bill Shock” and Cost Management
Unlike physical hardware where costs are fixed at purchase, cloud instances accrue charges every second they exist.

Leaving a 32-core instance with 128 GB RAM (r5.8xlarge, costing ~$2.00/hour) running over an unattended weekend costs $100. Leaving it forgotten for a month costs over $1,400 USD—a catastrophic blow to a small research grant.
The Solution: Automated shutdown scripts, spot instances, and hard budget alarms.

4. Data Sovereignty and Ethics
Storing human genomic or pathogen sequence data on commercial cloud servers located in US or European data centers may conflict with national data protection regulations or local research ethics protocols. Trainers should understand national health data laws and institutional compliance before migrating clinical data to commercial clouds.

13.4 Data Locality: Bring the Compute to the Data
The single most important computational principle in cloud bioinformatics is: Bring the compute to the data, not the data to the compute.



The importance of data locality


Because public repositories (NCBI SRA, ENA, 1000 Genomes, GISAID mirrors) are already mirrored in major commercial cloud storage buckets (AWS Open Data, Google Cloud Public Datasets), launching an analysis inside that same cloud region enables faster internal transfer speeds (often exceeding 10 Gbps) with zero data transfer fees.

text:
13.5 Cost Optimization: Making Cloud Affordable on a Grant
Bioinformatics workloads are typically batch-oriented and fault-tolerant. Thus, trainers must understand how to minimize expenditure:
1. Spot and Preemptible Instances (70–90% Discounts)
Cloud providers have excess server capacity. They auction this unused capacity as Spot Instances (AWS) or Spot/Preemptible VMs (GCP/Azure) at discounts of up to 90% off standard on-demand prices.

The Catch: If the provider needs the capacity back, the instance can be reclaimed with a 2-minute warning.
Why it fits bioinformatics: For pipeline steps that write intermediate checkpoints, or batch jobs managed by workflow managers (Nextflow, Snakemake), spot instances offer immense cost savings.

2. Hard Budget Alerts and Automated Kill Switches
Never launch a cloud project without setting automated billing alerts:

CloudWatch / GCP Budget Alerts: Send immediate email and SMS alerts when spending reaches 50%, 80%, and 100% of a defined monthly threshold (e.g. $50).
Auto-Shutdown Daemons: Add a simple cron script that monitors CPU utilization; if CPU activity stays below 5% for 30 consecutive minutes, the VM automatically triggers sudo poweroff, stopping per-hour compute charges.

13.6 Cloud Strategies for Delivering Bioinformatics Workshops
When designing a workshop in a low-resource setting, how should instructors provide computational environments without asking students for credit cards or risking live installation failures?

Table 2: Classroom cloud architectures






Architecture
Best For




1. Galaxy Training Network (GTN)(usegalaxy.*)
Novices, wet-lab biologists, zero-command-line curricula


2. GitHub Codespaces / Gitpod(60 free core-hours/month)
Intermediate CLI/Python/R lessons; browser-based VS Code interface


3. Centralized Instructor VM(Single multi-user cloud host)
Advanced CLI/HPC courses; single large VM, students connect via SSH



Approach 1: The Public Galaxy Network (Zero Cost, Zero CLI)

Use established public Galaxy instances (usegalaxy.eu or usegalaxy.org).
Instructors can create Galaxy Training Groups, which grant students priority queue access and temporary quota increases during workshop hours.
Requires only a standard web browser on any device.

Approach 2: GitHub Codespaces (Free Browser-Based Linux)

GitHub provides every free user with 60 core-hours per month of browser-based cloud computing.
Trainees open a repository in their browser and instantly receive a fully functional, containerized Linux terminal and VS Code editor.
Eliminates Windows/macOS compatibility issues while consuming minimal bandwidth (only keystrokes are transmitted across the internet).

Approach 3: The “Single Big Classroom Server”

The instructor provisions a single high-memory cloud instance (e.g. 16 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM on an AWS EC2 instance).
The instructor creates individual user accounts for each student (user01, user02, etc.) with resource quotas.
Students connect via SSH or a browser-based terminal (ttyd or JupyterHub).
Cost: ~$1.50/hour total for the entire classroom of 25 students! The instructor stops the instance at the end of each day.

title: 13  Cloud-based Bioinformatics
text:
13.7 Interactive Exercises for Future Trainers
These exercises will test your ability to design cost-effective cloud training workflows and advise researchers on resource management.






ExerciseExercise 1 - Designing a Cost-Control Protocol to Prevent “Bill Shock”






A postgraduate researcher at your institution receives a $500 cloud credit grant for their master’s project analyzing 60 bacterial whole-genome sequencing isolates. They intend to spin up a high-memory AWS EC2 instance (m5.4xlarge, 16 vCPUs, 64 GB RAM, costing ~$0.77/hour on-demand).

If the student finishes their analysis on Friday evening but forgets to terminate or stop the instance before leaving for a 3 week field trip, calculate the total unexpected expenditure.
What three safeguards would you teach this student to put in place before launching their first cloud machine?
How does stopping an instance differ from terminating an instance in terms of ongoing costs?







HintHint






Remember that stopping an instance halts per-second compute charges, but attached storage volumes (EBS) still accrue monthly storage fees until terminated.










AnswerAnswer






13.7.1 Cost Analysis & Safeguards

Unexpected Cost Calculation:

3 weeks = 21 days = 504 hours.
\(504\text{ hours} \times \$0.77/\text{hour} = \$388.08\text{ USD}\).
Over 77% of the student’s entire $500 research grant would be consumed by idle compute while they were away in the field.

Three Mandatory Safeguards:

Set AWS Budget Alarms: Configure alerts at $50, $100, and $250 that send automated SMS and emails to both the student and supervisor.
Configure Auto-Stop Triggers: Set a CloudWatch alarm that automatically stops the instance if average CPU utilization drops below 3% for 45 minutes.
Use Spot Instances: For batch bacterial assembly, run on Spot pricing (~$0.23/hour instead of $0.77/hour), reducing costs by ~70%.

Stopping vs. Terminating:

Stopping: Shuts down the CPU and RAM. You pay $0 for compute, but you continue paying a small fee for the attached virtual hard drive (EBS volume, ~$0.08–$0.10/GB/month) so your files are preserved when you restart.
Terminating: Permanently destroys the instance and deletes attached storage. All ongoing charges stop completely.
















ExerciseExercise 2 - Choosing the Right Cloud Platform for Training






You are leading a 3 day training event for 20 clinical microbiologists and hospital laboratory technicians in West Africa. The goal is to teach genomic surveillance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Audience Profile: Strong clinical microbiology background, zero prior command-line experience, using hospital-issued Windows laptops with locked-down administrative privileges.
Venue: Unstable mobile Wi-Fi (3–5 Mbps shared).

Evaluate the following three options and recommend the most effective training vehicle:

Option A: Have participants install Ubuntu inside VirtualBox on their laptops.
Option B: Teach them to launch and configure AWS EC2 Linux instances using individual AWS accounts.
Option C: Use the public Galaxy platform (e.g. usegalaxy.eu) with pre-loaded shared histories.







AnswerAnswer






13.7.2 Evaluation & Recommendation

Option A (Local VirtualBox): Poor choice. Hospital-issued laptops typically block virtualization in the BIOS and prohibit installing hypervisors without administrative privileges. Downloading 4 GB VM images over 3 Mbps Wi-Fi will fail.
Option B (AWS EC2 from Scratch): Poor choice. Requiring 20 clinical novices to create individual AWS accounts, register credit cards, navigate the complex AWS Management Console, and configure SSH keys introduces overwhelming cognitive load completely unrelated to the workshop’s biological learning objectives.
Option C (Public Galaxy Platform): RECOMMENDED.

Zero local installation: Runs entirely in any standard web browser; hospital IT restrictions are bypassed.
Low bandwidth footprint: The 3 Mbps Wi-Fi only needs to transmit lightweight browser clicks.
Data locality: The trainer can pre-upload the bacterial FASTQ files into a shared Galaxy History beforehand. Trainees clone the history in one click without downloading or uploading a single megabyte.
Pedagogical alignment: Learners focus 100% on the biological questions (identifying beta-lactamase genes and resistance mutations) rather than wrestling with Linux syntax or cloud billing.

13.8 Summary






TipKey Points




Elasticity Solves Hardware Upfront Costs: Cloud computing replaces expensive physical servers with flexible, on-demand compute, insulating researchers from local equipment depreciation, power outages, and cooling infrastructure failures.
Match Service Model to Audience: Use SaaS (Galaxy) for wet-lab novices and clinical audiences; use PaaS (Google Colab, Codespaces) for lightweight scripting; use IaaS (AWS, GCP) for advanced pipelines and custom deployments.

title: 14  Using an HPC or Server for Training
text:
14.1 Introduction: The Centralized Server
When teaching bioinformatics in low-resource settings, one of the most consequential decisions an instructor makes is where the computational work will physically take place.
In an ideal world, every learner arrives with an identical, high-performance laptop running Linux or macOS, equipped with 16 GB of RAM and administrative rights. In low-resource environments, however, the classroom reality is radically heterogeneous:
If an instructor chooses to run software directly on student laptops, the workshop risks falling into hours of debugging installation: Day 1 is completely consumed by troubleshooting compiler errors, PATH configurations, Windows line endings, and failed Conda solves. By the time the first biological command is executed, students are exhausted.
Deploying a centralized server or High-Performance Computing (HPC) cluster has several operational advantages:
However, moving computation to a centralized server introduces a critical trade-off: you replace 25 isolated points of failure with a single, shared point of failure. If the server crashes, if the network switch drops, or if 25 students overwhelm the CPU simultaneously, the entire classroom halts.
As a trainer, your goal is to harness the power of centralized infrastructure while ensuring you’ve introduced safeguards to ensure uninterrupted learning.

Trainees bring personal laptops ranging from decade-old dual-core machines with 4 GB of RAM to modern Windows 11 ultrabooks burdened by third-party antivirus software.
Many clinicians and institutional researchers use locked-down laptops provided by hospitals or government ministries that prohibit software installation or command-line developer tools.
Operating systems vary wildly across Windows 10/11, legacy Windows 7, macOS (Intel vs. Apple Silicon M-series), and diverse Linux distributions.





Remote computing topology for training




Environmental Uniformity: Every trainee logs into the exact same Linux environment with pre-installed software, identical reference files, identical paths, and guaranteed reproducible behavior.
Hardware Equalization: A student on a $200 netbook with 2 GB of RAM has access to the same 32 CPU cores and 128 GB of RAM as a student on a high-end workstation.
Preservation of Cognitive Load: Learners focus their mental energy on biological concepts, data interpretation, and Unix command syntax rather than system-level packaging errors.

section: 14.2 Classroom Server Topologies: Choosing the Right Model
text:
14.2 Classroom Server Topologies: Choosing the Right Model
Instructors in low-resource settings can deploy centralized compute using three primary topologies, each with distinct advantages, infrastructure requirements, and vulnerability profiles:

Table 1: Comparative analysis of classroom compute topologies








Topology
Infrastructure Requirements
Primary Advantages
Critical Vulnerabilities & Risks




1. In-Room Local Server (LAN / Offline)
• Physical tower server or mini-PC• Local network switch or Wi-Fi router• Venue UPS / inverter
• Zero internet required; immune to fiber cuts• Blazing fast local data transfers• Zero cloud subscription costs
• Physical transport of hardware• Dependent on classroom power grid• Single physical point of failure


2. Institutional / Regional HPC (SLURM)
• Institutional cluster or regional HPC (e.g. CHPC, WACREN)• Stable outbound internet
• Massive compute and memory capacity• Exposes learners to real-world HPC workflows• Zero local hardware transport
• Campus Wi-Fi often blocks Port 22 (SSH)• Bandwidth latency and dropouts• Queue wait times during live class


3. Cloud Training Server (IaaS)
• Single large cloud VM (AWS, GCP, Hetzner)• Outbound internet access• Credit card / cloud grant
• Elastic, on-demand sizing (e.g. 32 vCPU, 64 GB RAM)• Disposable (destroyed after workshop)• Easy pre-workshop image cloning
• Dependent on continuous internet• Risk of “bill shock” if forgotten• International currency payment barriers



Model 1: The In-Room Local Server (The Offline “Cluster-in-a-Box”)
For venues with unpredictable internet, the in-room local server is the gold standard of resilient training.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   IN-ROOM LOCAL SERVER ARCHITECTURE                    │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                        │
│   [ Portable Server / Tower / NUC ]                                    │
│   • 16–32 Cores, 64 GB RAM, 2 TB NVMe                                  │
│   • Pre-configured with accounts, data, and web terminal               │
│   • Plugged into Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS)                    │
│                     │                                                  │
│                     ▼                                                  │
│   [ Local Gigabit Switch / Offline Wi-Fi 6 Router ]                    │
│   (No external internet connection required; local subnet 192.168.1.x) │
│         │                  │                  │                  │     │
│         ▼                  ▼                  ▼                  ▼     │
│   [ Laptop 01 ]      [ Laptop 02 ]      [ Laptop 03 ]      [ Laptop 25 ]
│   (Connects via browser to https://192.168.1.100 or local SSH)         │
│                                                                        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
In this architecture, the instructor brings a powerful portable workstation (such as an Intel NUC, a high-spec gaming laptop, or a compact tower server) directly into the room. The server is connected via Ethernet to an inexpensive Wi-Fi 6 router or gigabit switch.
Students connect to the local Wi-Fi network and access the server via its local IP address (e.g., 192.168.1.100). Because data packets never leave the room, the workshop proceeds seamlessly even if the entire university loses outbound internet connectivity.






TipThe Hardware Profile of a Portable Classroom Server



An instructor does not need a massive enterprise server rack to teach 25 students. A modern compact mini-PC (e.g. AMD Ryzen 9 or Intel Core i9 with 16–24 cores, 64 GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 2 TB NVMe SSD) costs under $1,000, weighs less than 1.5 kg, fits into a backpack, and draws under 120W of power—making it easily supported by a small consumer UPS or 12V vehicle battery inverter during blackouts.


Model 2: The Shared Institutional or Regional HPC Cluster
When teaching advanced workflows (such as genome-wide variant discovery across hundreds of samples, de novo assembly, or RNA-seq quantification) that exceed the RAM of a single standalone machine, tapping into a shared institutional or regional HPC cluster (governed by SLURM) becomes necessary.
However, using a production HPC for live training requires specialized operational negotiation with system administrators:

Never rely on the default public queue: In a standard academic queue, a student’s 10-second alignment test may sit in PENDING state behind a multi-day molecular dynamics simulation submitted by another research group.
Request a Dedicated Classroom Reservation: Work with HPC administrators at least 3 weeks prior to the workshop to configure a dedicated reservation:
# Administrator command creating a training reservation for 32 cores:
scontrol create reservation user=instructor,trainee01,trainee02,... \
         starttime=2026-11-10T08:00:00 duration=08:00:00 \
         nodes=node[01-02] flags=SPEC_NODES,OVERLAP reservation=workshop2026
Students then submit jobs directly into the reservation without queue delays:
sbatch --reservation=workshop2026 run_alignment.sh
Establish a Training Partition with Dedicated QoS: Alternatively, request a temporary training partition with a high-priority Quality of Service (QoS) that restricts maximum walltime to 30 minutes and caps jobs per user to prevent queue starvation.

Model 3: The Single Cloud Virtual Machine
If physical hardware transport is impossible and the training venue has reliable internet, launching a single multi-core cloud instance (e.g., AWS EC2 c6i.8xlarge with 32 vCPUs and 64 GB RAM) provides an instant, throwaway training environment.

Pre-Configure Once, Clone Infinitely: Build your environment on a base image, take a snapshot, and launch it the morning of the workshop.
Automated Teardown: Configure an automated cron job or AWS CloudWatch alarm to terminate or stop the instance if CPU utilization remains below 2% for 60 consecutive minutes, eliminating accidental weekend “bill shock.”
